embedding-models-make-or-break-your-ai-a.problem: Retrieval systems quietly return the wrong context because the embedding model, chunk boundaries, and evaluation were never designed together.

terms.definition: A model that turns a piece of text into a fixed-length list of numbers, placing texts with similar meaning close together in that numeric space.
terms.why: Its geometry is the floor every retrieval result stands on, and swapping it later invalidates every stored vector.

terms.definition: A slice of a source document that is embedded, stored, and retrieved as one unit.
terms.why: A boundary through the middle of a fact makes that fact unretrievable regardless of how good the encoder is.

terms.definition: Running dense vector search and keyword search over the same document collection, then merging both ranked candidate lists into one.
terms.why: Dense search misses exact codes and rare jargon that keyword matching catches, so the merge widens what can be found.

terms.definition: A model that reads a query and one candidate passage together and scores how well they match, rather than comparing vectors computed separately.
terms.why: It reorders the candidate set for precision, but it cannot recover an answer that retrieval never surfaced.

arc: Retrieval quality is set before the model is chosen
Embeddings fix meaning in a geometry that cannot be mixed
Chunking, hybrid search, and reranking decide what is findable
Measure recall and precision, then fix the failing stage
embedding-models-make-or-break-your-ai-a.primer: Retrieval quality comes from a small set of moving parts: the encoder that places text in space, the pieces you store, and the extra passes that reorder them. Knowing which part owns which failure is what separates a demo from a system that stays correct.
embedding-models-make-or-break-your-ai-a.outro: Multimodal and long-context encoders remove preprocessing steps and make chunking less brittle, but they do not remove the need to measure what retrieval missed. As model quality converges across vendors, the durable advantage sits in chunk design, index migration discipline, and per-stage evaluation. Retrieval quality becomes an observability problem: knowing which stage failed rather than which benchmark won.
next: Build 150 query and answer pairs from real traffic, then record context recall and precision before changing any component.
Re-chunk one table-heavy document with headers repeated on every row and compare retrieval for a query that targets a single cell.
Run a second embedding model against a shadow index on sampled traffic before committing to a full migration.

temporal-primer.problem: Multi-step processes lose their place when a worker crashes mid-flight, forcing teams to build ad hoc status tables, retry loops, and sagas.

terms.definition: A runtime that records each completed step of a program so a new process can continue from the last recorded step after a crash instead of starting over.
terms.why: It is the property that lets a payment, provisioning, and email sequence survive a process death without duplicating effects.

terms.definition: The requirement that the same recorded history always leads the workflow code to make the same decisions, with anything that could vary moved outside it.
terms.why: Replay only works if re-running the orchestration code reproduces the original sequence of decisions.

terms.definition: A unit of work that touches the outside world, such as an API call, a database write, or an email, and may fail or return a different result on each attempt.
terms.why: Side effects live here so the orchestration layer can stay safe to replay while the platform retries the unreliable parts.

terms.definition: The append-only record of every decision, activity result, timer, and signal in one workflow execution.
terms.why: Recovery replays this record rather than restoring a snapshot, which is why changing workflow code can break in-flight runs.

arc: A crash between steps leaves partial work and no safe restart
Persist every decision as history and replay it
Keep orchestration deterministic and side effects in activities
Version workflow code like a schema migration
temporal-primer.primer: Long-running processes fail at the seams between steps, and the vocabulary below is what makes those seams explicit. The distinction that matters most is between code that decides and code that touches the world.
temporal-primer.outro: Durable execution turns recovery into a platform property, making agentic and financial workflows cheaper to operate but not free: history limits, versioning discipline, and replay cost remain real constraints. As more agent runtimes adopt the model, the interesting work moves to tooling that catches non-determinism before deploy and to patterns for workflows that live for years. Adoption is usually less urgent than deciding which processes deserve durability at all.
next: Rewrite one approval flow currently driven by a cron job as a workflow with a durable timer and a signal.
Add a version gate around a planned activity rename, then replay a recorded history against the new code.
Track event counts on a long-running workflow and trigger continue-as-new before roughly 10,000 events.

rag-production.problem: Indexes drift out of date and retrieval failures look like model failures because nothing connects a bad answer to the chunks that produced it.

terms.definition: A pattern where the application first fetches relevant passages from its own document collection and places them in the instructions sent to the model, so it answers from supplied text rather than memory.
terms.why: It splits the system into an offline indexing pipeline and an online query pipeline, and most production failures live in the first.

terms.definition: The slice of a document that gets embedded, stored, and retrieved as one unit.
terms.why: Chunk boundaries decide which facts can be surfaced, and chunk IDs are what an update or delete has to track down.

terms.definition: A small table mapping each source document to the IDs of its current chunks, so old vectors can be found and removed.
terms.why: Vector stores have no parent-document concept, so updates and deletes leave orphans or ghosts without this mapping.

terms.definition: A stable name that points at one concrete index, so a complete rebuild can be validated and then switched in a single step.
terms.why: It is what prevents a crashed re-index from leaving queries reading a mixture of document versions.

arc: A demo corpus hides freshness and deletion problems
Indexing needs a registry, hashes, and atomic swaps
Retrieval needs hybrid search and reranking
Traces must name chunks and index versions
rag-production.primer: A production retrieval system is two pipelines and a paper trail: one that builds and maintains the index, one that answers queries, and a record that lets you tell them apart when quality drops. The vocabulary below is the minimum needed to reason about freshness, deletion, and blame.
rag-production.outro: Better encoders and longer context windows reduce chunking pressure but do not remove the need for a registry, a deploy story, or chunk-level evidence. The next frontier is automatic attribution: linking each retrieved chunk to answer quality at request level and feeding that signal back into indexing. Teams that instrument now can adopt new models without guessing whether quality moved.
next: Add a registry table and a delete path to one existing index, then verify a deleted document stops appearing in results.
Record chunk IDs, scores, and index version on every retrieval and replay a week of bad answers through that data.
Build a full replacement index and switch the read alias only after a fixed benchmark query set passes.

structure-of-llm-chat.problem: Chat applications fail in confusing ways because the role-tagged message list, its serialization, and its token costs are treated as a display detail.

terms.definition: The exact text markers a model was trained to see around each role, such as special start and end tokens, applied before the model reads the conversation.
terms.why: A local model given the wrong markers produces quietly worse output instead of an error.

terms.definition: The message the application sets before the user speaks, carrying the assistant's role and tone, what it may answer, the required output format, and what to do when unsure.
terms.why: It is the strongest behavioural lever available, while still not being a security boundary.

terms.definition: An interface that keeps no memory between calls, so every request must resend the conversation needed to answer.
terms.why: It explains why token cost grows with every turn and why history is something the application edits.

terms.definition: Starting the assistant's reply with a few characters already in place so the model continues from that point instead of choosing its own opening.
terms.why: It constrains the first token of structured output when instructions alone have been unreliable.

arc: Roles are trained structure, not presentation
The system prompt steers but does not secure
Every call resends the history
Serialize, version, and validate the format
structure-of-llm-chat.primer: A chat request is a list of role-tagged messages that gets flattened into one token sequence before the model sees it. The terms below separate what the model was trained to expect from what the application must enforce.
structure-of-llm-chat.outro: As context windows grow and providers hide more serialization, the failure modes move from format bugs to history management: what to keep, summarise, or drop. Prompt injection remains outside what any template can fix, so the durable work is versioned prompts, output validation, and permissions enforced beneath the model. Chat interfaces may look simpler while the message list becomes a more deliberate artifact.
next: Print the raw serialized prompt for one local model and compare its markers with the format that model was trained on.
Split a production system prompt into persona, scope, format, and fallback sections and store it under version control.
Add a fixed set of 20 representative turns and run it before and after the next prompt change.

how-llms-work.problem: People treat language models as knowledge stores or creativity dials and are surprised when the same prompt gives different, sometimes false, answers.

terms.definition: A word or word fragment that the model reads and writes; text is split into tokens before prediction and joined back afterwards.
terms.why: Every cost, context limit, and generation step is measured in these units.

terms.definition: The raw score the model gives each possible next token before those scores are turned into probabilities.
terms.why: Temperature acts directly on these scores, which is why it changes the choice without changing knowledge.

terms.definition: The operation that turns raw scores into probabilities by exponentiating each one and dividing by their total, so the values are positive and sum to one.
terms.why: It is the step that creates the distribution the model samples from.

terms.definition: A number that divides the raw scores before softmax; below one sharpens the distribution toward likely tokens, above one flattens it toward unlikely ones.
terms.why: Choosing it per task is the difference between stable extraction and varied prose.

arc: One operation: predict the next token
Raw scores become a distribution you sample from
Temperature reshapes the distribution, not the knowledge
Test across runs and verify facts
how-llms-work.primer: Almost every surprising behaviour of a language model follows from how one next-token prediction is turned into a choice. These terms cover the path from raw scores to a sampled word, which is where temperature and reliability live.
how-llms-work.outro: Understanding sampling makes reliability an engineering problem: fixed settings, repeated runs, and validation around anything factual. It does not turn the model into a database, and no prompt removes the need to check names, numbers, and citations. The useful direction is systems that combine probabilistic generation with deterministic checks and retrieval.
next: Run the same extraction prompt ten times at temperature 0.2 and count how often the output parses.
Compute softmax by hand for three logits at temperatures 0.5, 1, and 2 to watch the probability mass move.
Add a verification step for every number or citation a model returns before it reaches a user.

monolith-is-distributed-system.problem: A monolith with one shared database carries the coordination and failure costs of a distributed system while hiding them from the team.

terms.definition: The degree to which one part of a system must change when another part changes, whether through a function call, a shared table, or a shared library.
terms.why: It is the real measure of whether an architecture behaves like a distributed system, independent of how many deployable pieces it has.

terms.definition: The promise a database's tables and columns make to every piece of code that reads them, whether or not that promise is written down.
terms.why: In a monolith it is implicit and unversioned, so a column rename becomes an invisible broadcast to unknown consumers.

terms.definition: A sequence of calls where each step waits for the next and the whole operation fails if any step fails.
terms.why: Function calls feel free, so these chains grow until one dependency can stop an entire operation.

terms.definition: An enforced limit on what one part of the code may call or read, strong enough that crossing it fails or requires deliberate review.
terms.why: A box-and-arrow diagram without enforcement stops matching the code as soon as a deadline arrives.

arc: One schema couples every feature area
Diagrams do not enforce module boundaries
Synchronous chains inherit every failure
Audit real coupling, then give modules their own data
monolith-is-distributed-system.primer: Distribution is a property of coupling, not of process count, and the terms below describe the couplings a monolith can hide. Once they are named, the architecture diagram can be compared with the call graph and the query log.
monolith-is-distributed-system.outro: The point is not to split the monolith but to make its internal contracts as explicit as a service boundary would force them to be. That means table ownership, versioned shared utilities, and a real call graph somebody maintains. Teams that do this keep the deployment simplicity and lose the invisible failure propagation.
next: Count how many feature areas read each of your five largest tables and rank the tables by that count.
Generate the real call graph from imports and raw SQL queries, then list chains that cross more than four concerns.
Give one module write ownership of its tables and route another module's reads through an interface instead of the tables.

curse-of-dimensionality.problem: Adding features or dimensions makes nearest-neighbour search and local models degrade in ways that look like bugs rather than geometry.

terms.definition: The effect where, as dimensions grow, distances from a point to all other points become nearly equal, so nearest stops being a meaningful distinction.
terms.why: It is the mechanism that strips nearest-neighbour search and density-based clustering of their guarantees.

terms.definition: The number of independent directions in which the data actually varies, which is often far below the number of columns it is stored with.
terms.why: The difficulty of a learning problem depends on this, not on the raw feature count.

terms.definition: A skew in high-dimensional neighbour graphs where a few points appear as the nearest neighbour of many queries while most points are never returned.
terms.why: It explains why a handful of documents or embeddings answer most retrieval queries.

terms.definition: Multiplying data by a random matrix to produce fewer dimensions while approximately preserving the distances between points.
terms.why: It is the constructive escape hatch that lets retrieval shrink vectors without losing the neighbourhoods it depends on.

arc: More dimensions thin the data exponentially
Distances converge and neighbourhoods stop separating
Hubs and overfitting follow from the same geometry
Measure concentration, then reduce or change the metric
curse-of-dimensionality.primer: High-dimensional failure is geometric before it is statistical, and the terms below name the specific ways proximity breaks. They also mark the boundary between algorithms that rely on distance and those that rely on linear algebra.
curse-of-dimensionality.outro: The practical split is between distance-based components, which need reduction or a different norm, and linear-algebraic ones, which often benefit from extra dimensions. Deep models learn compact manifolds that sidestep much of the problem, but retrieval indexes and density estimators still need monitoring for concentration and hubs. The next step is measurement: distance histograms and retrieval-frequency distributions before any dimensionality change.
next: Plot the pairwise distance histogram at the dimension you actually serve and check whether it has collapsed into a narrow band.
Measure what fraction of embeddings accounts for most retrievals; a few hundred serving nearly everything indicates hubness.
Reduce with PCA to 90 to 95 percent explained variance, then re-measure recall instead of assuming it held.

defensive-databases.problem: Databases assume a careful deterministic caller, while agents issue novel queries, retry blindly, hold connections while thinking, and fail silently.

terms.definition: A stable identifier attached to a logical operation so the database can recognise a retry and refuse to apply the same write twice.
terms.why: Orchestrators deliver each step at least once, so retries are normal, and this is what collapses several attempts into one row.

terms.definition: Marking a row as deleted while keeping its data, usually with a flag and the identity of whoever removed it.
terms.why: It turns an agent's destructive mistake into a query about what was removed rather than an unrecoverable loss.

terms.definition: A table where changes are recorded as new rows and existing rows are never updated or removed, leaving a full history.
terms.why: For high-stakes state, it makes undo a projection over events instead of a restore from backup.

terms.definition: Granting a database role only the specific reads and writes it needs, so one mistake cannot reach the rest of the system.
terms.why: Application code cannot bind a general-purpose reasoner, so the database role has to cap the blast radius.

arc: Agent callers break the assumptions schemas were built on
Retries and bad reads need idempotency and reversible writes
Think time and fan-out exhaust connection pools
Constrain access and instrument queries at the database
defensive-databases.primer: The failure modes below are ordinary database concerns that become urgent once the caller can reason its way into an unexpected query. The terms describe the few mechanisms that keep an unreliable caller from turning a mistake into an incident.
defensive-databases.outro: The defensive layer is mostly existing database machinery, promoted from best practice to load-bearing infrastructure: roles, constraints, soft deletes, query tags. It does not make an agent correct; it bounds what a wrong step can do and leaves evidence behind. As agent counts grow, expect these patterns to move into platform defaults rather than per-team discipline.
next: Give one agent its own database role with statement timeouts and no delete grant, then run its normal task.
Add an idempotency key and a unique constraint to the write path that agents retry most often.
Tag agent queries with agent, task, and step IDs, then build a view of database time grouped by agent.

bm25.problem: Keyword search needs a ranking that rewards repetition and document length only up to a point, and simple term counting gets both wrong.

terms.definition: How many times a query word appears in a document, used as evidence that the document is about it.
terms.why: The first occurrences carry real signal, which is why counting them linearly over-rewards a repetitive page.

terms.definition: A weight that lowers the contribution of words appearing in many documents and raises it for words appearing in few.
terms.why: It is the part of the score that makes a rare product code matter more than a common word.

terms.definition: A curve where the first occurrences of a term add a lot of score and later ones add progressively less, approaching a ceiling; a parameter called k1 sets how quickly it flattens.
terms.why: It is the fix for a document that repeats a phrase forty times and would otherwise outrank a focused definition.

terms.definition: Adjusting a document's term evidence by how long it is relative to the average document in the collection; a parameter called b sets how strongly this is applied.
terms.why: Without it, a long chapter wins simply by containing more opportunities to mention the query.

arc: Counting terms linearly over-rewards repetition and length
Saturate term frequency and normalise by length
Rare terms carry more weight through IDF
Tune k1 and b, then combine with dense retrieval
bm25.primer: The score has three separable parts, repetition, rarity, and length, and each one is a tuning decision rather than a constant. The terms below name those parts so a surprising ranking can be traced to the one that caused it.
bm25.outro: BM25 remains the interpretable, exact-match leg of hybrid retrieval, and its limits are predictable enough to design around. Adding dense retrieval covers synonyms and intent, but fusion and reranking bring their own tuning and latency. The useful next move is to treat ranking as an observable system: inspect per-term scores, then change one parameter at a time.
next: Run explain on a surprising result and identify whether IDF, saturation, or length normalization produced the order.
Lower k1 for a corpus of short product titles and compare top-10 precision with the default.
Add BM25 as a second candidate list beside dense retrieval, fuse with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, then rerank.

join-algorithms.problem: A join can quietly compare every row of one table against every row of another, turning a fast query into a long scan.

terms.definition: The part of a database that estimates the cost of possible execution plans and picks the cheapest one. It uses table sizes, indexes, sort order, and available memory to choose a join method.
terms.why: Its cost estimate is what selects or rejects each join algorithm.

terms.definition: A join that builds an in-memory lookup table from the smaller input, then scans the larger input and probes that table for matches. It works only for equality joins and needs the build side to fit in memory.
terms.why: It is the default workhorse for large equality joins and the baseline the other algorithms are compared against.

terms.definition: A hash join that first partitions both inputs into matching buckets on disk, then joins one bucket pair at a time so each fits in memory. It trades extra disk reads for the ability to join inputs larger than memory.
terms.why: It is the fallback when the hash table cannot fit and the clearest case of paying I/O to escape a memory limit.

terms.definition: A distributed join that sends a full copy of the small table to every node, so each node can join its local slice of the large table without moving that large table across the network.
terms.why: It shows that in a cluster the deciding cost is network transfer, not comparison count.

arc: The naive join compares every row with every row
Each algorithm exploits order, hashing, an index, or partitioning
Memory, skew, and network transfer decide which one wins
Read the query plan and check the cost assumptions
join-algorithms.primer: The vocabulary here separates what a join costs in comparisons from what it costs in memory and network traffic. Once those are distinct, the planner's choice stops looking arbitrary.
join-algorithms.outro: Faster storage and distributed engines shift the balance but do not remove the core tradeoffs: a hash table still needs memory, a sort still costs time, and a broadcast still fills the network. The open problems are estimation and skew, because a planner that misjudges row counts or key distribution can pick a sound algorithm for the wrong size of data. The practical path is to read actual plans, measure spills and shuffles, and test the assumptions rather than memorizing a ranking of algorithms.
next: Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a join and identify the chosen algorithm, the estimated row counts, and any disk batches.
Create a test table with one dominant key and compare a hash join plan before and after the skew appears.
Estimate broadcast versus shuffle cost for a small dimension table against a large fact table at your real node count.

half-life.problem: Technical knowledge expires faster than a career, so staying useful requires a permanent learning budget rather than a one-time degree.

terms.definition: The time it takes for half of what a person knows in a field to be replaced or made obsolete. Shorter half-lives mean skills lose value faster.
terms.why: It turns skill decay into a measurable rate that can be compared across eras and specialties.

terms.definition: Concepts that stay useful across tools and languages, such as data structures, algorithms, distributed systems, and complexity. They explain why systems behave as they do.
terms.why: It is the layer that decays slowest and therefore deserves disproportionate investment.

terms.definition: Broad familiarity with many areas plus deep expertise in a few. The wide bar lets a person move between contexts; the deep stem gives them a specialty to apply.
terms.why: It is the proposed shape for surviving a short half-life without becoming a specialist tied to one stack.

arc: Knowledge decays on a clock measured in years
Frameworks expire faster than fundamentals
Experience stops compounding linearly with age
Budget weekly learning and favor transferable depth
half-life.primer: Three ideas carry the argument: a decay rate, a split between durable and perishable knowledge, and a shape for investing in both. They explain why seniority alone is not a stable advantage.
half-life.outro: AI tools compress the half-life further by automating the routine tasks that once trained juniors, while making experienced judgment more valuable. That does not make fundamentals obsolete; it raises the cost of acquiring them through ordinary work. The next question is personal and organizational: who pays for the learning hours, and how can deliberate practice be attached to real production problems instead of side projects.
next: List the skills used in the last month and mark each as foundational or tool-specific.
Block seven to ten hours a week for deliberate learning and protect them like meetings.
Pick one current production problem as the vehicle for learning a new tool, then write down the transferable pattern afterward.

multi-paxos.problem: Several database replicas must agree on one order of transactions even when messages are delayed, reordered, or lost and leaders crash.

terms.definition: A majority of the voting nodes, such as three out of five. Any two majorities share at least one node, so two conflicting decisions cannot both win.
terms.why: It is the overlap that lets the protocol stay safe while tolerating some failed nodes.

terms.definition: A number that identifies which leader is in charge. It rises when leadership changes and stays fixed while one leader keeps proposing.
terms.why: Reusing one ballot across many proposals is what removes the repeated prepare step.

terms.definition: The first round of Paxos, where a node asks a majority to promise not to accept older proposals. It reserves the right to propose and collects any value already accepted.
terms.why: Running it once per leader term instead of once per write is the central Multi-Paxos optimization.

terms.definition: An ordered list of operations that every replica stores in the same sequence. Applying the same operations in the same order leaves every replica in the same state.
terms.why: It converts agreement on single values into agreement on a transaction history.

arc: Independent Paxos rounds are too slow for a stream of writes
A stable leader keeps one ballot and skips repeated prepares
One round trip per write, but all writes funnel through one node
Batch, pipeline, and split hot ranges when the leader saturates
multi-paxos.primer: The terms describe a voting system with terms, promises, and a shared history. Keeping those three separate makes the difference between basic Paxos and Multi-Paxos easy to see.
multi-paxos.outro: Multi-Paxos guarantees that replicas never disagree, but it does not guarantee that progress happens within a fixed time; a partition can stall writes until it heals. Its stable leader also concentrates load, so the next problems are hot ranges, cross-region latency, and coordinating transactions that span several groups. Systems address those with range partitioning, read replicas, and two-phase commit layered on top, which is why the protocol survives as a component rather than a complete database design.
next: Trace one transaction through prepare, accept, commit, and apply, writing down which nodes persist what at each step.
Work out the failure tolerance of a three-node and a five-node group and the quorum each needs.
Compare the message count of basic Paxos and Multi-Paxos for a thousand writes under one stable leader.

mysql-replication-internals.problem: A second copy of a database must stay current without slowing the source or silently drifting out of sync.

terms.definition: An append-only record of every change made on a MySQL source, stored as events in numbered files. It is the source of truth that replicas read from.
terms.why: Every stage of replication is organized around moving and replaying these events.

terms.definition: A local copy of received events on a replica, written before those events are applied. It buffers the network receiver from a slower applier.
terms.why: It explains why a slow replica does not push back on the source and where a stalled apply can be inspected.

terms.definition: A binlog format that records the actual rows changed rather than the SQL statement that changed them. It is deterministic but larger when one statement touches many rows.
terms.why: The format choice decides whether a replica can reproduce the source exactly or may diverge on non-deterministic statements.

terms.definition: A mode where the source waits for at least one replica to confirm it received a transaction before reporting the commit to the client. A timeout falls back to asynchronous mode.
terms.why: It is the main lever for reducing the window where a committed transaction exists only on a source that then crashes.

arc: The source writes every change to an ordered log
The replica pulls events, buffers them, then applies them
Sequential apply becomes the bottleneck on a busy source
Parallelize safely, prefer row format, and watch lag
mysql-replication-internals.primer: The pipeline has four moving parts: a log on the source, a receiver on the replica, a buffer, and an applier. Naming them separately makes most replication symptoms point to a specific stage.
mysql-replication-internals.outro: Replication keeps a warm copy and enables read scaling, but asynchronous replay means the copy can lag and a failover can lose recent commits. Semi-synchronous mode narrows that window at the cost of latency, and multi-threaded apply narrows the lag at the cost of coordination. The idea leads toward change data capture, multi-source aggregation, and tested failover procedures, because a replica is only useful for availability if it can actually be promoted.
next: Run SHOW REPLICA STATUS and map each field to the receiver, relay log, or applier stage.
Compare binlog size and replica behavior for one large UPDATE under statement-based and row-based logging.
Set a semi-synchronous timeout in a test environment and observe what the source does when the replica stops acknowledging.

bloom-filters.problem: Tracking which items a system has already seen can need more memory than the machine has, even when an occasional wrong answer would be harmless.

terms.definition: A compact set-membership structure made of a bit array and several hash functions. It can say that an item is definitely absent or only that it might be present.
terms.why: It is the structure that replaces stored keys with a few bits per item.

terms.definition: A wrong answer that claims an item is in the set when it is not. A Bloom filter can produce these, but it never claims an item is absent when it was added.
terms.why: The acceptable rate of these errors is the budget that determines how much memory the filter needs.

terms.definition: A function that turns an input into a number in a fixed range. A good one spreads inputs evenly so the resulting positions look random.
terms.why: Each item sets several positions derived from hashes, so hash quality and count directly control collisions.

terms.definition: An immutable file of sorted key-value pairs on disk, written when an in-memory table fills up. A lookup may have to check several of these files.
terms.why: Attaching a filter to each file lets the database rule out a disk read before performing it.

arc: Exact membership sets grow past the memory budget
Hash each item into several shared bit positions
A zero proves absence, a one is only a maybe
Spend bits on the error rate the application can tolerate
bloom-filters.primer: The structure is easiest to grasp as an asymmetry: absence is certain, presence is a guess. The terms below cover the bits, the errors, the hashing, and the storage layout where the guess pays off.
bloom-filters.outro: A Bloom filter is the right tool when a false positive costs a retry or an extra lookup and a false negative would be a correctness bug. It does not solve deletion, counting, or exact answers; those need counters, region tracking, or the original data. As datasets outgrow memory, the same idea increasingly sits in front of disk reads, network shuffles, and cache decisions, which is why the next step is usually to measure the real false-positive rate rather than trust the formula.
next: Compute the bits per element needed for a one percent and a zero-point-one percent false-positive rate at your expected item count.
Benchmark insert and lookup throughput with two hash functions versus the optimal k for your data size.
Add a filter in front of a large join or a multi-file lookup and measure how many expensive reads it avoids.

clock-sync-nightmare.problem: Machines cannot agree on the current time, yet databases, logs, and build tools treat timestamps as if they were a reliable global order.

terms.definition: The difference between two clocks at the same instant. It grows from temperature changes, manufacturing variation, and aging in the quartz oscillator.
terms.why: Skew is what silently reorders events and makes a timestamp comparison wrong.

terms.definition: A protocol that periodically asks hierarchical time servers for the time and adjusts the local clock. Its accuracy is limited by uneven network delay in each direction.
terms.why: It is the default synchronization layer whose millisecond accuracy is enough for some systems and not others.

terms.definition: A range of times guaranteed to contain the true time, rather than a single reading. A system can wait until the whole range has passed before treating a timestamp as ordered.
terms.why: It is how TrueTime converts an imprecise clock into a strong ordering guarantee at the cost of a short wait.

terms.definition: A counter that orders events by causality instead of wall-clock time. It increases on local events and on message receipt, so a cause always has a lower value than its effect.
terms.why: It offers ordering without synchronized hardware, but cannot tell whether two events were concurrent.

arc: Quartz clocks drift and no global clock exists
Skew silently reorders events instead of raising errors
Sync protocols, logical clocks, and bounded time buy different guarantees
Choose the weakest clock that meets the ordering requirement
clock-sync-nightmare.primer: The vocabulary separates physical error, network correction, causal order, and bounded uncertainty. Each answers a different question, and mixing them up is how systems acquire ordering bugs that look like data corruption.
clock-sync-nightmare.outro: Perfect synchronization is impossible, so the practical goal is a known error bound rather than a perfect clock. Better hardware and cloud time services shrink that bound, but they do not remove the need to decide whether an application needs causal order, real-time order, or only approximate timestamps. The idea leads toward hybrid clocks, leap-second handling, and monitoring for backward jumps, because a clock that moves unexpectedly can break assumptions that no protocol-level fix will catch.
next: Measure the offset between two machines you operate and compare it with the ordering precision your application assumes.
Use a monotonic clock for measuring durations and reserve wall-clock time for display and audit records.
Write down whether a given feature needs causal order, total order, or only approximate time, then pick the clock mechanism from that answer.

kafka-partitions.problem: Adding partitions to a Kafka topic looks like a routine scaling command but permanently changes which consumer sees which key.

terms.definition: An ordered, append-only slice of a topic. Each partition is stored on a broker, and messages within one partition are read in the order they were written.
terms.why: It is both the unit of parallelism and the unit that preserves order for a key.

terms.definition: A set of consumers that share the work of reading a topic. Each partition is assigned to at most one consumer in the group at a time.
terms.why: The group's maximum parallelism is capped by the partition count, which is the usual reason to add partitions.

terms.definition: The producer-side logic that chooses a partition for each message. With a key, it hashes the key and takes the remainder against the partition count.
terms.why: Changing the partition count changes that remainder, so the same key can move to a different partition.

terms.definition: The process of redistributing partitions among consumers when the group or the partition count changes. Older protocols paused all consumers; newer ones move only the partitions that must move.
terms.why: It determines how much processing stops during and after an expansion.

arc: Partitions cap parallelism and fix key placement
Expansion changes the hash modulus for every key
Old messages stay put while new messages move elsewhere
Migrate through a new topic or accept and repair ordering
kafka-partitions.primer: Four terms explain the whole ripple effect: the slice, the group that reads it, the function that assigns keys to slices, and the reshuffle when assignments change. The command is small; the contract it alters is not.
kafka-partitions.outro: Partition count behaves like a long-lived schema decision because offsets, key placement, and consumer state all depend on it. Expansion preserves old data and idempotent produce semantics, but it cannot preserve per-key order across the boundary or move state stores with their keys. That pushes stateful systems toward new topics and planned migrations, and it makes over-partitioning early cheaper than repairing a broken ordering contract later.
next: Calculate the partition count needed for your target consumer parallelism and expected peak throughput, then add headroom.
Map a sample of real keys to partitions under the current and proposed counts to see which keys move.
Run a rebalance in a test group with the cooperative sticky assignor and measure the pause per partition.

product-quantization.problem: A billion high-dimensional vectors do not fit in memory at full floating-point precision, which makes exact nearest-neighbor search impractical on ordinary hardware.

terms.definition: Representing a vector by the nearest point from a fixed, finite set instead of storing all its coordinates. The replacement point is an approximation, so some detail is lost.
terms.why: It is the basic move that turns storage into a small identifier rather than a full vector.

terms.definition: A representative point learned from a cluster of similar vectors. A collection of centroids used for quantization is called a codebook.
terms.why: Each chunk of a vector is replaced by its nearest centroid's index, which is where the compression comes from.

terms.definition: A slice of the vector's dimensions, such as dimensions one through sixteen of a 128-dimensional vector. Product quantization treats each slice as its own smaller quantization problem.
terms.why: Splitting into subspaces is what avoids needing an impossibly large single codebook.

terms.definition: The fraction of truly nearest neighbors that a search actually returns. Compression lowers recall because approximate distances can rank some true neighbors below other vectors.
terms.why: It is the cost side of the memory savings, and the reason compressed indexes are used to generate candidates rather than final answers.

arc: Raw float vectors exhaust the memory budget
Split each vector into chunks and store a centroid ID per chunk
Codes shrink sixty-fourfold but distances become approximate
Over-fetch candidates and rescore with full vectors
product-quantization.primer: The method is a chain of three reductions: a vector becomes chunks, a chunk becomes a centroid ID, and a distance becomes a table lookup. The terms below name each reduction and the accuracy it costs.
product-quantization.outro: Product quantization makes billion-scale search fit on commodity machines, but it does not preserve exact distances and its error grows as codes get smaller. The practical consequence is a two-stage search: a compressed index proposes candidates, and full-precision vectors or a reranker decide the final order. The idea leads toward combining quantization with graph or inverted-file indexes, tuning the number of candidates, and measuring recall against latency rather than assuming compression is free.
next: Compute the raw and compressed index size for your vector count, dimensions, and chosen number of subspaces.
Measure recall at several candidate counts against an exact search on a sample, then choose the smallest count that meets your target.
Compare asymmetric distance computation with decoding each code and computing the distance directly.

qkv-matrices.problem: A model must decide which words in a sequence matter to each other without reading them one at a time and forgetting the distant ones.

terms.definition: A mechanism that lets each position in a sequence look at every other position and combine their information according to relevance. It replaces step-by-step recurrence with direct comparison.
terms.why: It is the operation that the three matrices exist to feed.

terms.definition: A learned numeric vector that represents a token, such as a word, in a high-dimensional space. Similar meanings tend to land near each other.
terms.why: The input matrix is a stack of embeddings, and Q, K, and V are projections of it.

terms.definition: Multiplying an input vector by a learned weight matrix to produce a new vector in a different space. The weights are trained rather than hand-set.
terms.why: Q, K, and V are three different projections of the same token embeddings, which is why one input yields three views.

terms.definition: A function that turns a list of raw scores into positive weights that sum to one. Larger scores get disproportionately larger weights.
terms.why: It converts query-key similarity scores into the proportions used to mix value vectors.

arc: Recurrence processes tokens one at a time
Project each token into a query, a key, and a value
Compare queries with keys, then mix the matching values
Split into heads and stack layers to capture more relations
qkv-matrices.primer: The three matrices are easiest to hold together as a lookup: a query asks, a key advertises, and a value carries content. The terms below cover that analogy, the vectors being projected, and the step that turns scores into weights.
qkv-matrices.outro: Q, K, and V are only the setup; the ranking comes from scaled dot products, softmax, and a weighted sum of values. That design lets a model relate distant tokens in one step, but it also makes every token compare with every other, so cost grows with sequence length. The idea leads toward multiple heads, efficient attention variants, and inspection of attention patterns to understand what a model actually uses.
next: Construct Q, K, and V by hand for a three-word sentence with small matrices and verify every shape.
Compute the score matrix, apply softmax, and check that each row's weights sum to one.
Vary the projection width and count how the parameter total and attention cost change.

how-llm-inference-works.problem: A single LLM request is slow for two different reasons: the prompt pass saturates compute while token-by-token generation waits on memory, so one latency fix rarely helps both.

terms.definition: The first pass over the whole prompt, where all input tokens are processed at the same time. It is compute-heavy because the GPU is doing large matrix multiplications.
terms.why: It sets the wait before any output appears and is the phase where more compute actually helps.

terms.definition: The second stage, where the model produces one token at a time and each token depends on everything before it. It is memory-bound because every step moves large weight matrices for very little arithmetic.
terms.why: It determines how smoothly text streams and why a faster GPU alone may not speed up generation.

terms.definition: Stored copies of the key and value vectors for tokens already processed, kept so attention does not recompute them for every new token. It grows with context length and occupies GPU memory.
terms.why: It is the biggest single speedup in inference and the reason long prompts can exhaust memory.

terms.definition: Storing weights, and sometimes cached values, in lower-precision numbers such as 8-bit or 4-bit integers instead of 16-bit floats. It shrinks memory and bandwidth at a small cost in accuracy.
terms.why: It is how a 7B model drops from about 14 GB to 3.5 GB and fits on smaller hardware.

arc: Prompt tokens are processed in parallel and saturate compute
Generation switches to one token at a time and stalls on memory traffic
The KV cache removes recomputation but consumes GPU memory
Tune each phase and measure time-to-first-token against inter-token latency
how-llm-inference-works.primer: Inference splits into two phases with opposite bottlenecks, plus one cache and one precision choice that decide whether the model fits at all. These four terms are what the rest of the discussion assumes.
how-llm-inference-works.outro: Serving frameworks now compete on cache management and batching rather than raw arithmetic, which pushes the interesting engineering into memory layout and scheduling. Longer contexts make cache size the binding constraint, so expect more work on paging, prefix sharing, and lower-precision caches. None of that changes the fundamental split: prefill stays compute-bound and decode stays bandwidth-bound, and both still have to be measured separately.
next: Measure time-to-first-token and inter-token latency separately on one real prompt before changing any hardware.
Quantize a 7B model to INT4 and record both the memory drop and any change in answer quality.
Compare vLLM with continuous batching against a naive generation loop on the same GPU.

blocking-queues.problem: Hand-written locks and polling around a shared buffer produce busy-waiting, unbounded memory growth, and shutdown paths that leak waiting workers.

terms.definition: A queue whose add and remove operations wait instead of failing when the queue is full or empty. The calling thread sleeps until there is space or an item, then continues.
terms.why: That single change replaces explicit lock and condition-variable choreography with one wait.

terms.definition: A queue with a fixed maximum capacity, allocated up front. Once it is full, producers must wait, so memory use cannot grow with the backlog.
terms.why: The bound is what turns an overloaded pipeline into slower producers rather than an exhausted process.

terms.definition: The signal that travels back to a producer when the consumer cannot keep up. In a bounded queue it appears as a blocked write rather than as growing memory.
terms.why: It is the mechanism that makes overload visible to whoever is submitting work.

terms.definition: A lightweight unit of concurrent execution in Go, scheduled by the language runtime rather than the operating system. A blocked one is cheap but still holds its state.
terms.why: Every unclosed channel leaves a goroutine waiting, which is the leak the shutdown rules exist to prevent.

arc: A plain queue fails or returns empty instead of waiting
A blocking queue parks the caller until space or data exists
The bound turns overload into backpressure instead of memory growth
Shutdown paths and depth metrics keep the queue from leaking or stalling
blocking-queues.primer: The vocabulary here is about who waits and what stops the waiting. Once those roles are clear, every producer-consumer arrangement is a variation on one contract.
blocking-queues.outro: The same contract underpins worker pools, pipelines, and request queues, so the design question moves from synchronization to sizing and shutdown. In production, queue depth becomes an operational signal: a depth that only rises points at consumers, not at producers. The unresolved part is choosing the bound, which depends on measured latency rather than on any formula.
next: Replace one unbounded buffer with a capacity chosen from peak observed queue depth.
Add a close path and a cancellation signal to every consumer, then verify no goroutine remains after shutdown.
Export queue depth as a metric and alert when it stops draining under normal load.

heartbeats-in-distributed-systems.problem: A distributed system cannot directly observe a dead node, only silence, and every rule for turning silence into failure misreads either real crashes or ordinary network delay.

terms.definition: A small message a node sends on a fixed schedule to say it is still running. A monitor records the last one it saw and treats silence past a threshold as a possible failure.
terms.why: It is the only signal the rest of the failure-detection design is built on.

terms.definition: A failure detector that reports suspicion as a continuous number instead of alive or dead. It learns the usual spacing of heartbeats and raises the score as one arrives later than expected.
terms.why: It replaces one hand-tuned timeout with a confidence level that adapts to each node's network.

terms.definition: A way for nodes to spread membership information by periodically swapping what they know with a few random peers. No central monitor is needed, and news reaches everyone gradually.
terms.why: It lets failure detection scale without a single monitor becoming the bottleneck.

terms.definition: The smallest number of nodes that must agree before the cluster takes an action such as electing a leader or accepting a write. In a five-node cluster that number is three.
terms.why: It is what stops both sides of a partition from acting as if the other side were dead.

arc: Silence has to stand in for failure
Interval and timeout trade detection speed against false alarms
Adaptive detectors and gossip spread the judgment across the cluster
Quorum decides which side is still allowed to act
heartbeats-in-distributed-systems.primer: Failure detection moves from a single signal to a cluster-wide judgment, so the terms progress from one heartbeat to the rules built on top of it.
heartbeats-in-distributed-systems.outro: Once failure detection is probabilistic, the interesting design work moves to consequences: who may act, and how quickly the rest of the cluster learns. Gossip keeps detection flat as clusters grow, but it trades immediacy for eventual agreement, which is why quorum rules sit underneath leader election. The next layer is separating suspicion from permission, so a slow node does not trigger a split-brain response.
next: Derive a timeout from measured round-trip time and count consecutive misses instead of one gap.
Track the false-positive rate of node-down alerts for a week and compare it with the configured threshold.
Trace one partition scenario in a test cluster and confirm the minority side stops accepting writes.

cassandra-writes.problem: Cassandra must accept writes quickly across many machines while letting each client choose how much replica agreement to wait for before the write counts as successful.

terms.definition: The value Cassandra hashes to decide which nodes own a row. Every read and write for that row goes to the same small set of replicas.
terms.why: It determines both where a write lands and whether the load spreads across the cluster.

terms.definition: An append-only file on disk that records each write before it is applied in memory. It is replayed after a crash to recover writes that had not yet reached a table file.
terms.why: It is the durability guarantee behind the fast acknowledgement.

terms.definition: The number of replicas that must acknowledge an operation before the node handling the request answers the client. ONE, QUORUM, and ALL are points on that scale.
terms.why: It is the dial that trades write latency and availability against how many copies must agree.

terms.definition: A saved note a coordinator keeps when a replica misses a write, replayed if that replica returns within a time window. It is best-effort and does not replace repair.
terms.why: It covers a reboot without making the write wait for a down node, but expires after a long outage.

arc: Any node can coordinate, and the partition key picks the replicas
The write appends to a log and an in-memory table before the ack
Consistency level decides how many replicas must answer
Hints and repair handle replicas that missed the write
cassandra-writes.primer: A Cassandra write is one sequence with a decision point near the end, so these terms follow the order a mutation travels.
cassandra-writes.outro: Because every write is an append and every replica receives it in parallel, throughput scales with partitions rather than with node count alone. The cost appears later, as compaction, repair, and clock discipline, which are operational commitments rather than configuration details. The next question is how reads reconcile the versions that writes leave behind.
next: Trace one insert through coordinator, replicas, CommitLog, and MemTable on a test cluster.
Compare p99 write latency at ONE, LOCAL_QUORUM, and QUORUM for the same workload.
Check NTP drift on every node and confirm it stays under 500 ms.

redis-replication.problem: Redis promises sub-millisecond operations, and a replication design that made replicas poll for updates would add a round trip and idle traffic to every write.

terms.definition: A model where the main server, called the primary, sends each write to its replicas as the write happens, instead of waiting for them to ask. Delay is then mostly network time.
terms.why: It is the choice that keeps replication lag in milliseconds rather than seconds.

terms.definition: A fixed-size circular buffer on the primary holding recent write commands. A replica that reconnects can resume from an offset if it is still inside this window.
terms.why: It decides whether a brief disconnect costs a cheap resume or an expensive snapshot.

terms.definition: The first synchronization, where the primary snapshots its dataset, buffers writes made during the snapshot, sends the snapshot, then replays the buffer. Later writes stream one by one.
terms.why: Its cost is why backlog sizing and diskless transfer matter for recovery time.

terms.definition: How far a replica is behind the primary, measured in bytes of the command stream or in time. It is normally milliseconds but has no fixed upper bound.
terms.why: It is the gap that makes replica reads potentially stale and failover potentially lossy.

arc: Polling would add a round trip and a wait to every update
The primary streams each write immediately over a persistent connection
A backlog makes short disconnects cheap but slow replicas expensive
Lag guards and WAIT expose the asynchrony that remains
redis-replication.primer: The argument runs from latency to the primary's resource budget, so the terms describe the stream, its buffer, and the gap it can leave.
redis-replication.outro: Push keeps lag small but leaves replication asynchronous, so replica reads can still be stale and a failover can lose the last writes. Backlog size becomes the knob that decides whether a network blip costs a resume or a full snapshot. The next step is deciding which reads can tolerate that gap and which must go to the primary.
next: Measure master and replica offsets during a traffic spike to see the real lag in bytes.
Raise repl-backlog-size and test whether a thirty-second disconnect avoids a full resync.
Add min-replicas-to-write and confirm how the primary behaves when replicas fall behind.

cdn-content-replication.problem: Serving every request from one distant origin makes first delivery slow, and copying content to hundreds of locations raises the question of what to copy, where, and when to replace it.

terms.definition: A server close to users that stores copies of content so requests do not travel to the origin, the source server that holds the original. A CDN runs many of them, each with limited storage.
terms.why: Placing a copy at the edge removes the round-trip distance that dominates a first request.

terms.definition: The identifier an edge uses to look up a stored response, normally the URL plus selected headers. If the key includes a content hash, new bytes become a different object.
terms.why: It is what makes a deploy create a new object instead of serving a stale one under the same name.

terms.definition: How long an edge may serve a stored copy before checking with the origin. A short lifetime keeps versions fresh at the cost of more origin requests.
terms.why: It is the alternative to purging when content changes often.

terms.definition: An instruction to invalidate a cached object everywhere. It propagates gradually, and the next request at each edge fetches the object again from the origin.
terms.why: Its uneven propagation and simultaneous refetches are the failure mode the rest of the design works around.

arc: Distance and handshakes dominate the first request
Copies move closer by push, pull, or a hybrid of both
Hashes and lifetimes decide when a copy counts as current
Propagation delay and origin egress set the bill
cdn-content-replication.primer: Replication is a policy per object rather than one global setting, so the terms describe the copy, its identity, and its expiry.
cdn-content-replication.outro: Once edges also run code, replication covers behaviour as well as bytes, and cache hit rates depend on how much of a response is dynamic. The open problem is not making propagation instant but making the window of mixed versions safe for the application. That shifts design effort toward versioned URLs and short, deliberate lifetimes rather than hoping a purge lands everywhere at once.
next: Put a content hash in one asset URL and confirm a deploy creates a new cache object without any purge.
Replace one purge with a short TTL plus stale-while-revalidate and compare origin load.
Measure origin egress before and after narrowing which objects are pushed to every edge.

grpc-http2.problem: gRPC has to carry many concurrent calls and long-lived streams between services, while HTTP/1.1 gives each connection only one request at a time.

terms.definition: Sending many independent request and response streams over one network connection at the same time. Frames from different calls are interleaved instead of queued one behind another.
terms.why: It removes the need for large connection pools and stops one slow call from blocking unrelated ones.

terms.definition: One logical call inside an HTTP/2 connection, identified by an ID. Frames carry that ID, so both sides can send data for several calls without confusion.
terms.why: A bidirectional gRPC call maps directly onto one stream, which is why streaming fits the transport.

terms.definition: The header compression scheme in HTTP/2. It keeps a table of headers already seen and sends a short index for repeats instead of the full text.
terms.why: It makes the metadata forwarded on every service hop nearly free.

terms.definition: A limit on how many bytes a sender may have in flight before the receiver acknowledges them. It protects the receiver's memory and gives streaming a natural brake.
terms.why: It is what stops a fast producer from exhausting a slow consumer during a stream.

arc: One request per connection forces pools and queues
Frames and stream IDs let many calls share a socket
Compressed headers and flow control cut overhead and protect memory
The trade is setup cost and harder debugging for one-off calls
grpc-http2.primer: The connection savings come from transport mechanics rather than from the RPC framework itself, so these are the features that make many calls share one socket.
grpc-http2.outro: The connection savings matter most in dense service graphs, where sockets and handshakes were the hidden tax on every call. HTTP/2 does not remove the need to think about payload size or stream lifetimes, and binary framing makes some failures harder to see. The next layer is stream-aware load balancing, which is still uneven across proxies.
next: Count TCP connections per peer in a service mesh before and after consolidating onto HTTP/2.
Run a bidirectional streaming call with a slow consumer and watch WINDOW_UPDATE frames arrive.
Time one small request over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 to see where HTTP/2 loses.

why-consensus.problem: Several replicas can each accept a valid-looking write, and without a shared decision rule they can end up with different histories.

terms.definition: A protocol that gets a group of machines to agree on one value or one order of events, even when some of them fail or cannot communicate.
terms.why: It is the difference between independent replicas and one system with a single history.

terms.definition: The promise that nothing contradictory is ever decided. Two nodes cannot settle on different values, and no accepted decision is later reversed.
terms.why: It is the guarantee that keeps a replicated balance from being spent twice.

terms.definition: The promise that the system eventually makes progress. A decision is reached rather than postponed forever.
terms.why: It is the separate promise that stops a safe protocol from simply refusing to decide.

terms.definition: The smallest majority of nodes allowed to act on the cluster's behalf. Requiring it means only one side of a split can continue.
terms.why: It turns a partition into a slowdown on one side instead of divergence on both.

arc: Replicas accept writes independently and diverge
Partitions, crashes, delay, and clock skew defeat simple ordering
Consensus separates safety from liveness and uses a majority to act
The same guarantee sits inside databases, queues, and cluster managers
why-consensus.primer: Two words are often confused in this area, so the terms separate what must never happen from what must eventually happen, then add the rule that makes both possible.
why-consensus.outro: Consensus turns agreement into a reusable component, which is why most teams meet it through etcd, Kafka, or a database rather than by writing Raft. The remaining judgment is scope: which state truly needs one order and which can tolerate a stale read. Getting that boundary wrong adds latency without buying correctness.
next: List the state in one system that requires a single order and the state that can be eventually consistent.
Trace a leader election in etcd or Kafka and identify the quorum that makes it valid.
Write down the expected behaviour of the minority side of a three-two partition.

database-deadlocks.problem: Concurrent transactions that take the same rows in different orders eventually form a circular wait, and no amount of testing removes the possibility.

terms.definition: A cycle of transactions each holding a lock the next one needs, so none can proceed. It is a property of the order locks were taken, not of any single statement.
terms.why: It explains why the fix is structural ordering and retries rather than a patch to one query.

terms.definition: A graph where transactions are nodes and an edge means one is waiting on another. A cycle in it is a deadlock.
terms.why: It is how the database finds the cycle and chooses which transactions to break apart.

terms.definition: When a database replaces many fine-grained row locks with one coarser table lock to save memory. It can pull unrelated transactions into a conflict.
terms.why: It is one reason a deadlock can appear between statements that never name the same rows.

terms.definition: The transaction a database aborts to break a deadlock. Its work is rolled back, and the application is expected to retry.
terms.why: Its selection decides how much work is lost and whether retries make progress.

arc: Inconsistent lock order closes a cycle
The wait-for graph finds cycles on a schedule
A victim is aborted and its work rolled back
Consistent ordering, short transactions, and whole-transaction retries reduce the damage
database-deadlocks.primer: Detection is a graph problem and resolution is a choice, so the terms are the parts of the cycle and the decision that breaks it.
database-deadlocks.outro: Deadlocks remain a scheduling problem rather than a bug class, so the durable fixes are structural: one lock order, short transactions, and retries at the transaction boundary. Detection policy then becomes a tuning choice between CPU spent checking and time spent waiting. The next useful signal is the deadlock log, which names the statement pair that closed the cycle.
next: Enable deadlock logging and collect the statement pairs from one week of production traffic.
Impose one lock order on the two code paths that touch the same rows.
Wrap multi-row writes in a retry that restarts the whole transaction with backoff.

cpu-cache-locality.problem: Code that performs the same number of operations can run an order of magnitude slower because of the order in which it touches memory.

terms.definition: The fixed-size block, typically 64 bytes, that a processor moves from main memory into its cache in one go.
terms.why: The 64-byte fetch is why column-major traversal wastes 15 of every 16 integers it loads.

terms.definition: The tendency to reuse the same memory address soon after touching it.
terms.why: It explains why a small hot counter stays fast while a single pass over a huge array gains nothing from reuse.

terms.definition: The tendency to touch memory addresses that sit close together.
terms.why: Row-major traversal and the Redis eviction pool are both bets that nearby addresses will be needed together.

arc: Fast memory is small
Cache lines and two kinds of locality
Loop order versus operation count
Measure misses before trusting Big O
cpu-cache-locality.primer: Two access patterns can execute the same instructions and still differ by an order of magnitude, because the processor moves memory in blocks and guesses ahead. These terms describe the guess, the two ways it pays off, and the unit that makes wasted fetching visible.
cpu-cache-locality.outro: Thinking in locality turns performance work from counting operations into arranging data so the fast tiers keep answering. It does not remove the need for a sound algorithm, and it does not tell you which layout wins without measurement. The next step is to profile real access patterns, then try tiling, prefetching or an array-backed structure where the misses concentrate.
next: Profile a matrix traversal with perf and compare L1 miss rates for row-major and column-major loops.
Rewrite one hot loop with tiling so each block fits in a cache level, then measure the change.
Find a linked structure on a hot path and test an array-backed replacement against it.

eventual-consistency.problem: A system spread across regions cannot keep every copy perfectly synchronized without paying in latency and uptime, so it must decide what to sacrifice during a partition.

terms.definition: The claim that a distributed system facing a network partition must give up either consistency or availability.
terms.why: The three-way trade-off is why partition tolerance is treated as mandatory and consistency becomes the variable.

terms.definition: Every copy of the data returns the same value once a write completes, as if there were only one copy.
terms.why: It is the baseline whose latency and availability costs the rest of the argument is measured against.

terms.definition: Copies may disagree for a while, but with no new writes they converge to the same value.
terms.why: Convergence without a deadline is what turns staleness into a product decision rather than a correctness checkbox.

terms.definition: A data type whose concurrent updates can be merged automatically in any order without coordination.
terms.why: It is one of the concrete merge mechanisms that lets writes proceed on separate nodes and combine later.

arc: Partitions are unavoidable
Consistency versus availability
Convergence without a deadline
Choose per operation, hide the delay
eventual-consistency.primer: The choice only becomes clear once the CAP properties and the two consistency models are kept distinct, because most design mistakes come from collapsing them into one decision. These terms carry the trade-off from theory down to a single read or write.
eventual-consistency.outro: Accepting eventual consistency moves the hard problem from replication into product design: each read path must state how stale its data can be, and interfaces must absorb the gap. It does not make conflicts disappear, since concurrent writes still need ordering or merge rules, and it remains the wrong default for balances and payments. The reasoning leads next into how many copies a read must contact, conflict resolution and per-operation consistency budgets.
next: List every read path in one service and write down the maximum staleness each can tolerate.
Prototype an author-sees-own-write path and measure how many strong reads it removes.
Compare a vector-clock merge with a CRDT merge for one data type the system already stores.

dns-udp-tcp.problem: Treating DNS as a UDP-only protocol leaves a system unable to resolve large or signed answers, usually discovering it only when those queries time out.

terms.definition: A connectionless transport that sends independent datagrams with no handshake and no session state.
terms.why: Ordinary lookups are two stateless packets, which is why the fast path avoids connection setup entirely.

terms.definition: A connection-oriented transport that establishes a session and delivers data reliably and in order.
terms.why: It is the fallback that carries oversized answers and zone transfers when UDP cannot.

terms.definition: A flag in a DNS response saying the answer did not fit, so the client should retry over TCP.
terms.why: It is the normal handoff signal, not an error, and a resolver that ignores it returns incomplete answers.

terms.definition: An extension that lets a DNS client advertise a UDP response buffer larger than the original 512-byte limit.
terms.why: It raises the practical ceiling to 4096 bytes, though network equipment in between still fragments or drops packets that large.

arc: DNS is not UDP-only
Why the fast path is stateless
When the answer outgrows the datagram
Open and monitor both transports
dns-udp-tcp.primer: The transport choice stays invisible until an answer grows too large, and then a UDP-only path fails in a way that looks like an ordinary timeout. These terms cover the fast path, the handoff and the configuration that keeps both paths working.
dns-udp-tcp.outro: Seeing DNS as a two-protocol system turns it into a capacity and firewall concern: small queries pass while signed or oversized zones fail quietly. It does not remove the latency cost of fallback, which is paid on each miss unless the resolver remembers what needs TCP. The next step is to monitor fallback rates and response sizes, then give both transports enough headroom.
next: Confirm that port 53 is open for both UDP and TCP through every firewall and load balancer on the path.
Query a DNSSEC-signed name and a large TXT record, then verify the resolver retries over TCP.
Add a dashboard for UDP success rate, TCP fallback frequency and response-size distribution.

okr.problem: Teams copy their task backlog into OKRs, so the framework reports activity instead of whether anything meaningful changed.

terms.definition: A short qualitative statement of where a team wants to go during a cycle.
terms.why: It states the destination the quarter is organized around and sets up the test of whether it inspires anyone.

terms.definition: A measurable change that shows whether the objective was reached.
terms.why: The measurable half is where a task list most often disguises itself as a goal.

terms.definition: Work that was completed, such as shipping a feature, as opposed to a change in a business metric.
terms.why: Separating completed work from changed numbers is the test the whole review pass applies.

arc: Goals drift into task lists
Objectives name a destination
Key results must move a number
Cut the count and review drafts
okr.primer: The framework is easy to imitate badly: the labels are simple to copy while the measurement quietly disappears. These terms separate the destination, the evidence of arrival and the activity that too often replaces both.
okr.outro: Good OKRs turn a quarter into a few falsifiable bets, which makes trade-offs visible and lets engineering and product argue about the same business result. They do not fix a team that cannot choose priorities, and a metric can still be gamed when it is easy to move but unrelated to the objective. The next step is to run the same checks at the start of every cycle and keep scoring focused on impact rather than completion.
next: Rewrite one current key result that reads like a ticket as the measurable change it is meant to produce.
Audit the quarter's OKRs for any result that could reach 100% while its objective still fails.
Compare engineering and product OKRs and mark where the business outcome does not map one-to-one.

theta-sketches.problem: Distinct-count sketches answer how many unique items a stream contains but cannot answer overlap or exclusion questions across streams.

terms.definition: A fixed-size summary that estimates how many distinct items a stream contains without storing the items themselves.
terms.why: It is the family of bounded-memory summaries whose accuracy and memory costs set up the comparison.

terms.definition: A compact sketch, often shortened to HLL, that estimates distinct counts and merges by union but cannot intersect or subtract.
terms.why: It is the efficient default for counting and the baseline that justifies paying more for set operations.

terms.definition: A number between 0 and 1 that sets how much of the range of hash values a sketch keeps; the retained count divided by it estimates the total.
terms.why: A shared threshold is what makes two independently built sketches comparable.

terms.definition: Operations that combine two sets into a new one: union, intersection and difference.
terms.why: Audience overlap and exclusion are exactly the questions that a count-only sketch cannot express.

arc: Distinct counts are not enough
Sample hashes under a threshold
Filter both sides to the smaller theta
Pay for algebra only where overlap matters
theta-sketches.primer: Choosing a sketch is really choosing which questions the system will be able to answer later. These terms separate a counter from a composable sample, which is the distinction the sizing and accuracy rules rest on.
theta-sketches.outro: Theta sketches turn audience overlap into a query-time merge instead of a scan, at the cost of roughly thirty times the memory of a comparable HLL. They do not rescue tiny intersections, where the retained sample becomes too small to estimate, and they cannot answer whether one specific user was present. The next step is to size the sketch from the intersection you expect, fix the hash seed across services, and pre-compute sketches where queries will combine them.
next: For one audience query, compute the ratio of union size to intersection size and check the expected error at the current sketch size.
Store a Theta sketch per dimension value at ingestion and compare query latency with an exact count.
Fix and document one hash seed across every service that will exchange sketches.

3p.problem: Deciding whether to change jobs by feel produces either inertia or a rash move, with no way to review the decision later.

terms.definition: Pay: salary, bonus and the rate at which compensation grows.
terms.why: It is the dimension most visible from outside and the easiest to trade away for the other two.

terms.definition: Growth in core competence: harder problems and deeper domain skill, not a larger team or a bigger title.
terms.why: It separates real skill growth from a prestigious role that leaves competence unchanged.

terms.definition: Upward movement on the org ladder, measured by title, responsibility and a credible promotion path.
terms.why: It captures ladder progress, which can stall even while the day-to-day work feels busy.

arc: A vague urge to leave
Score pay, growth and ladder
Two of three is enough
Re-score every six months
3p.primer: A job decision becomes reviewable once the vague dissatisfaction is split into three dimensions with different time horizons. The terms below are the whole framework; the judgement lies in which two are actually being served.
3p.outro: Scoring the three Ps turns a career move into an explicit trade, so lower pay or a flat title can be defended rather than drifted into. It does not tell you what the market will pay or whether a promised promotion is real, and the weighting stays personal. The next step is to write down the current pair every six months and compare it with what the role actually delivered.
next: Name the two Ps the current role served over the last six months, with one piece of evidence for each.
Check the market rate for your level and compare it with current pay.
Ask for the concrete promotion criteria and the date of the next review.

on-demand-container-loading-in-aws-lambd.problem: Large container images make cold starts slow because the function waits for bytes it may never touch before it can begin executing.

terms.definition: The delay before a function begins handling a request when no warm instance is already available.
terms.why: It is the latency the design protects while deployed images grow to 10 GiB.
