terms.definition: Fetching only the chunks of a container image that execution touches, instead of transferring the whole image first.
terms.why: It is the mechanism that lets the function start before the rest of its image arrives.

terms.definition: Encrypting each chunk with a key derived from its own content, so identical content produces identical encrypted output.
terms.why: It keeps duplicate blocks detectable across encrypted containers without a central key store.

terms.definition: Splitting data into pieces plus extra recovery pieces so the original can be rebuilt from a subset of them.
terms.why: It replaces full replicas with cheaper redundancy that also helps route around a slow shard.

arc: Bigger images, slower starts
Fetch blocks as they are touched
Deduplicate and encode for redundancy
Trade salt and redundancy against risk
on-demand-container-loading-in-aws-lambd.primer: The design only makes sense once the bytes a function needs at startup are separated from the bytes in its image. These terms cover the latency target, the loading mechanism and the two storage tricks that make the approach economical.
on-demand-container-loading-in-aws-lambd.outro: On-demand loading shifts the cold-start budget from total image size to the first working set, so deployment size can grow without a proportional startup penalty. It does not remove the need to keep startup reads small, and the deduplication that saves storage concentrates risk in widely shared chunks. The next step is to inspect what a large artifact actually reads at startup and whether a shared base layer already covers most of it.
next: Measure which files a service reads in its first second of startup and compare that with total image size.
Check whether the base image is shared across functions and estimate the deduplication win.
Model how many workloads would share a popular chunk before deciding how aggressively to rotate the salt used when deriving keys.

sql-has-problems-we-can-fix-them-pipe-sy.problem: SQL's fixed clause order runs backwards from the order data actually flows, so complex queries turn into nested subqueries that are hard to read and debug.

terms.definition: The `|>` symbol that feeds the table on its left into the operation on its right.
terms.why: It is the syntax that lets a query be written in the order the engine executes it.

terms.definition: An operation that takes exactly one table as input and returns exactly one table.
terms.why: That contract is why stages can be reordered, repeated and extended without hidden dependencies.

terms.definition: The guarantee that stopping a query after any stage still leaves a valid query over the intermediate table.
terms.why: It is what makes a half-written query runnable for inspection instead of forcing a separate subquery.

terms.definition: A function that returns a table, so it can be used wherever a table is expected.
terms.why: `CALL` shows how such a function becomes an ordinary pipeline stage rather than a nested special case.

arc: Clause order fights data flow
Each stage transforms one table
Truncate the query to debug it
Adopt pipes as an extension
sql-has-problems-we-can-fix-them-pipe-sy.primer: The proposal adds little new capability; it makes an existing pipeline visible in the order it runs. These terms describe the unit of composition, the guarantee that makes it safe, and the debugging payoff that follows.
sql-has-problems-we-can-fix-them-pipe-sy.outro: Pipe syntax turns query authoring into a sequence of inspectable steps, lowering the cost of reading, testing and extending a complex statement. It does not change what the query computes, and authors still need to know which stage belongs where. The next step is to convert one painful query stage by stage and compare each intermediate table with what the old query produced.
next: Rewrite one nested query as a pipe sequence and stop after each stage to inspect the rows.
Add a DESCRIBE or LOG stage to a query whose intermediate schema is unclear.
Take a table-valued function already in use and replace its nested call with a CALL stage.

nanolog-a-nanosecond-scale-logging-syste.problem: Conventional logging formats strings, takes locks and writes to disk on the application's critical path, making each call far too expensive for latency-sensitive code.

terms.definition: The code that runs on every request or event, where added latency is felt directly by users.
terms.why: It is the part of execution whose time the design refuses to spend on formatting or I/O.

terms.definition: A fixed-size queue that wraps around and reuses its slots instead of allocating new memory.
terms.why: A per-thread queue removes locks and allocation from every log call.

terms.definition: A slowdown where two threads update separate variables that sit in the same small block of memory, so the hardware keeps invalidating the block between cores.
terms.why: It is the hidden cost that remains after locking is gone, which padding the producer and consumer state addresses.

terms.definition: Writing values as their raw bytes instead of converting them into readable text.
terms.why: Keeping arguments in binary defers the expensive conversion to text until after execution.

arc: Logging costs land in the hot path
Move format work to compile time
Record into per-thread buffers
Defer formatting and emission
nanolog-a-nanosecond-scale-logging-syste.primer: The speedup comes from moving work in time rather than making each individual step faster. These terms identify what stays on the critical path, where records go, and why the layout of the buffer still matters.
nanolog-a-nanosecond-scale-logging-syste.outro: Deferring formatting and I/O turns logging into a bounded append plus background work, which changes what latency-sensitive services can afford to record. It does not make logging free: buffer capacity and emission throughput still set limits, and the deferred step must still reconstruct order and readable text. The next step is to find the logging call on a measured hot path and ask which parts of it could happen later.
next: Benchmark the current logger against an append-only binary record on the hottest request path.
Inspect a multi-threaded log buffer for fields written by different threads that share a cache line.
Estimate log volume per second and check whether a single emission thread can drain it.

wtf-the-who-to-follow-service-at-twitter.problem: Twitter's Who to Follow service had to suggest relevant accounts from a follower graph too large for ordinary disk-backed processing while still answering in milliseconds.

terms.definition: Twitter's custom graph engine that keeps users and their follow relationships in memory on one machine.
terms.why: It is the engine that made the whole follower graph fit and be traversed without disk reads or network hops.

terms.definition: A traversal that starts at one user and repeatedly steps to a randomly chosen account they follow, with many runs counting how often each account is reached.
terms.why: Repeated walks from a user turn raw follow edges into a ranked list of nearby accounts to recommend.

terms.definition: An algorithm that scores points in a graph split into two sides, such as users and content, by passing scores back and forth between the sides.
terms.why: It supplied the global influence signal that local walks could not provide, so authoritative accounts surfaced in recommendations.

terms.definition: A graph whose points fall into two groups, where connections run only between the groups and never within one.
terms.why: The user-and-content split is what lets SALSA score influence separately from neighbourhood proximity.

arc: A follow graph is too large to traverse from disk per request
Keep the whole graph in memory on one server
Walk locally for neighbours, score globally for influence
Partition the graph once it outgrows one machine
wtf-the-who-to-follow-service-at-twitter.primer: Four ideas carry the design: an in-memory graph engine, random walks for local neighbourhoods, and a two-sided ranking method for influence. Together they explain why a recommendation service can stay simple for years and then need a rewrite.
wtf-the-who-to-follow-service-at-twitter.outro: The single-server design shows that centralization is a legitimate strategy while the working set fits in memory, not a mistake to avoid on principle. It does not remove the ceiling: memory capacity and repair time eventually force a distributed rewrite, and that rewrite introduces partitioning, replication and failover. The next step is to treat the migration as part of the design, so the graph format and query layer can survive the move.
next: Estimate the memory needed per user and per follow edge, then compare it with the RAM of one large machine.
Implement a short random walk over a small graph and inspect how visit counts rank nearby nodes.
Read the original WTF paper and compare its first-generation and second-generation architectures.

structure-your-design-interviews.problem: Open-ended system design prompts tempt candidates to start drawing components immediately and run out of time before covering trade-offs.

terms.definition: A deliberately simple first-pass architecture that ignores scaling, replication and failure handling.
terms.why: The schedule uses an early day-0 sketch to expose your approach while there is still time to correct it.

terms.definition: A choice to give up one property, such as simplicity or low latency, in exchange for another.
terms.why: The follow-up block is where you justify the trade-offs behind each component you drew.

terms.definition: The ability of a system to keep serving when a component crashes or a network link fails.
terms.why: The hardening phase asks you to rearchitect the design around crashes, overload and network failures.

arc: An open prompt has no single correct answer
Buy constraints before drawing components
Sketch a naive design, then harden it under failure
Spend the last block on follow-ups and detail
structure-your-design-interviews.primer: Three ideas make the schedule usable: a rough first design, the failure cases that harden it, and the trade-offs you must defend. They matter because the interview is judged on the discussion, not on a finished diagram.
structure-your-design-interviews.outro: A fixed clock turns the interview into a sequence of decisions the interviewer can follow and redirect. It does not guarantee the right architecture, because the quality of the clarifying questions and the depth of the hardening still carry the result. The same structure transfers to design reviews and architecture discussions, where an early sketch and an explicit trade-off list move a group faster than a polished diagram.
next: Run a 45-minute mock interview with a timer split into the five phases.
Write down five clarifying questions you would ask for a URL shortener before drawing anything.
Take one component and list three failure modes with the change that addresses each.

keep-yourself-unblocked.problem: Engineers lose days to blocks that could be resolved faster by asking, shrinking the problem, or escalating a dependency.

terms.definition: A situation where you cannot make progress because an answer, decision or another team's work is missing.
terms.why: The whole practice is about recognising a block early and choosing a route out instead of sitting in it.

terms.definition: Goodwill and familiarity built with teammates before you need a favour from them.
terms.why: Existing rapport is what makes a request for help get a faster response when you are stuck.

terms.definition: Breaking a large problem into smaller pieces that can each be checked on their own.
terms.why: It converts an overwhelming block into a sequence of small questions, each with a visible result.

terms.definition: Raising a stuck dependency to a manager or other authority after normal requests have failed to move it.
terms.why: It is the last route for a block owned by another team, where working harder on your side cannot help.

arc: Being stuck is normal; staying stuck is costly
Try the cheapest route first
Explain, detour, decompose, then escalate
Learn so the same block does not recur
keep-yourself-unblocked.primer: The vocabulary here is about routes out: a block, the rapport that makes asking cheap, the decomposition that makes a problem testable, and escalation when another team owns the dependency. The order matters more than any single technique.
keep-yourself-unblocked.outro: Unblocking is a repeatable practice rather than a personality trait, so the useful change is to make the routes explicit and cheap to use. It does not eliminate hard problems or guarantee that help arrives quickly, especially across team boundaries. Over time the stronger move is to remove the recurring cause, whether that is missing documentation, an unclear ownership boundary, or a dependency that needs a service-level agreement.
next: Write a one-paragraph template for asking a teammate for help that includes what you already tried.
Pick one current block and shrink it to a single testable question.
List the dependencies your team does not own and who to contact for each.

genetic-knapsack.problem: Exact dynamic programming for 0/1 knapsack slows down as capacity grows, so large instances need a fast approximation that is good enough rather than optimal.

terms.definition: Choosing a subset of items, each taken whole or not at all, to maximise total value without exceeding a weight limit.
terms.why: It is the packing problem the genetic algorithm is being used to approximate.

terms.definition: A running time that grows with the numeric value of an input such as capacity, rather than with how many digits that value takes to write.
terms.why: It explains why the exact O(n·W) solution collapses on large capacities and why an approximation is worth accepting.

terms.definition: A score that rates how good a candidate solution is and therefore guides which candidates are kept.
terms.why: Selection, survival and the final answer all depend on it, and a badly chosen score optimises the wrong property.

terms.definition: Combining parts of two parent solutions to produce new candidate solutions.
terms.why: It is the variation step that lets the population explore packs neither parent contained.

arc: Exact dynamic programming is pseudo-polynomial in capacity
Encode packs as bit strings and score them
Select, cross over, mutate, and reproduce
Cap the generations for a predictable cost
genetic-knapsack.primer: Four ideas carry the method: the packing problem, the runtime trap in its exact solution, the score that ranks candidates, and the mixing operator that creates new ones. They explain how a search can improve without ever proving it found the best pack.
genetic-knapsack.outro: The genetic algorithm trades the optimum for a runtime you can predict from population size, generation count and fitness cost, which is what makes it usable on large or multi-dimensional instances. It does not tell you how close the answer is to optimal, and a poorly chosen fitness function will quietly optimise the wrong property. The same loop extends to problems with several constraints, where the fitness function has to encode every constraint deliberately.
next: Implement the four-item example and plot average fitness across 500 generations.
Change the fitness function to reward unused capacity and observe which packs survive.
Run the same instance with two-point crossover and compare its convergence with single-point crossover.

pseudorandom-number-generation-lfsr.problem: Simple devices need cheap random-looking numbers, but a generator that repeats too soon or can be predicted from its output is unfit for the job.

terms.definition: A row of bits that shifts one place on each step and fills the empty end with a bit computed from the others.
terms.why: It is the whole generator: cheap in hardware and software, and deterministic from its starting state.

terms.definition: The starting bit pattern loaded into the register, which determines the entire sequence that follows.
terms.why: The same seed reproduces the same bits, which is useful for scrambling and simulation and dangerous for secrecy.

terms.definition: A bit position whose value is combined with the output bit to compute the feedback bit.
terms.why: The set of taps, together with the seed, decides how long the sequence runs before it repeats.

terms.definition: The number of steps before the register returns to its starting pattern and the output begins to repeat.
terms.why: A short period makes the stream obviously non-random, so tap and seed choice have to be checked before use.

arc: Randomness here is deterministic, not true
Shift bits and feed back an XOR of taps
Seed and taps set the cycle length
Use it for scrambling, never for secrets
pseudorandom-number-generation-lfsr.primer: The terms are mechanical: a register of bits, the seed that starts it, the taps that decide its feedback, and the period before it repeats. They matter because the same few parts explain both the generator's efficiency and its predictability.
pseudorandom-number-generation-lfsr.outro: The generator is attractive where cost and reproducibility matter more than unpredictability: embedded code, simulation and simple scrambling. It does not provide security, because a short run of output is enough to solve for the internal state, and a poorly chosen tap set shortens the cycle until the stream repeats. The next step is to treat seed and tap selection as part of the design, then test the period and linearity before trusting the output anywhere sensitive.
next: Build the four-bit LFSR with seed 0b1001 and tap 1, then confirm the stream repeats after 15 steps.
Try several tap positions on an eight-bit register and record the cycle length for each.
Scramble a small file with the generator and verify that running the same function restores it.

how-indexes-work-on-partitioned-and-shar.problem: Once data is partitioned by one key, queries on any other attribute either scan every partition or need an index designed for that access pattern.

terms.definition: A lookup structure that maps a non-primary attribute to the identity of the records that hold it.
terms.why: It is how a query by genre finds movies when the collection is partitioned by movie ID.

terms.definition: An index built separately inside each partition, covering only the records that partition owns.
terms.why: It keeps writes local and cheap, but a query without the partition key must visit every partition.

terms.definition: An index over the whole dataset, partitioned by the indexed attribute rather than by the base table's key.
terms.why: It makes a global query single-partition, at the cost of coordinating index updates across nodes.

terms.definition: Sending one query to many partitions and combining their answers.
terms.why: It is the expensive read path that a local index forces when the partition key is missing.

arc: Partition-key lookups hit one node
Other attributes need a secondary index
Local indexes write cheaply but read narrowly
Global indexes read widely but pay on writes
how-indexes-work-on-partitioned-and-shar.primer: The distinction to hold onto is where the index lives: inside each partition or across the whole dataset. That single choice decides whether a query touches one node or many, and whether writes stay local or become a distributed transaction.
how-indexes-work-on-partitioned-and-shar.outro: Local and global indexes are not competing defaults; they encode different assumptions about which queries must be fast. Local indexes keep writes cheap and fail when the partition key is missing, while global indexes make the indexed query local at the cost of synchronous distributed writes or asynchronous staleness. The practical next step is to derive the index layout from the query set, then decide explicitly whether readers can tolerate a lag measured in seconds to minutes.
next: List the top five queries for a partitioned table and mark which ones include the partition key.
Sketch a local and a global index for a genre query, then trace the read path for each.
Estimate how many extra remote writes a synchronous global index adds per base write.

some-data-partitioning-strategies-for-di.problem: A database outgrows one node, and the way its keys are split decides whether load spreads evenly or piles onto a few hot partitions.

terms.definition: The attribute whose value decides which partition owns a record.
terms.why: Both range and hash strategies operate on it, and its choice determines which queries can stay local.

terms.definition: Giving each partition a continuous slice of the key space, such as keys beginning with A through F.
terms.why: It keeps keys ordered and routing deterministic, but a time-ordered range can absorb every new write.

terms.definition: Running the key through a function that turns it into a spread-out number, then using that number to choose the owning partition.
terms.why: It spreads writes statistically instead of maintaining range boundaries, at the cost of ordered access.

terms.definition: A partition that receives far more traffic or data than the others because the split ignored how the data is accessed.
terms.why: It is the failure mode both strategies are judged against, since idle nodes do not help a skewed workload.

arc: Partitioning helps only when load is balanced
Ranges give ordered scans and deterministic routing
Hashing spreads writes but scatters order
Pick the split from the access pattern
some-data-partitioning-strategies-for-di.primer: Two placement strategies and one failure mode are enough to follow the comparison: contiguous ranges, hashed keys, and the skew that appears when either ignores how the data is actually read and written. The trade-off between ordered scans and even spread is the thread through every card.
some-data-partitioning-strategies-for-di.outro: Neither strategy wins outright: ranges keep scans local and invite hot edges, while hashing spreads writes and makes range queries fan out. The design question is therefore not which algorithm is better but which queries must stay cheap and which can afford to touch many partitions. Composite keys are the common next move, using one part for placement and another for order inside a partition.
next: Take a time-series workload and explain why per-day range partitions concentrate writes.
Hash a sample of keys into ten buckets and check the bucket sizes for skew.
Design a composite key for a chat app that keeps one user's messages ordered on one partition.

data-partitioning.problem: A single database hits hardware limits on reads, writes and availability, so its data has to be split across machines without losing locality or recoverability.

terms.definition: The attribute used to decide which segment owns each record.
terms.why: Deterministic placement and single-partition queries both depend on choosing and supplying it.

terms.definition: Splitting different rows of a table across partitions, so each node holds a subset of records.
terms.why: It is the usual route to spreading read and write load beyond one machine.

terms.definition: Splitting different columns into separate partitions, so each partition holds a subset of fields.
terms.why: It is the contrasting split for warehouses, where queries touch only a few columns.

terms.definition: Keeping copies of each partition on additional nodes so a lost copy can be recovered.
terms.why: Partitioning limits the blast radius of a failure; replication is what turns that limit into availability.

arc: Vertical scaling ends at a hardware ceiling
Split rows across partitions by a key
Localized queries hit one partition and writes spread
Replicate each partition to survive a node loss
data-partitioning.primer: The core vocabulary separates three moves that are easy to blur: splitting rows, splitting columns, and copying partitions. Keeping them apart explains why partitioning scales throughput while replication is what actually protects availability.
data-partitioning.outro: Partitioning converts one machine's ceiling into a cluster's capacity, and replication converts a node failure from data loss into a recoverable event. It does not make cross-partition queries free, and a poor partition key can still concentrate load on one node. The next design question is how partitions are rebalanced and how replicated copies stay current, which is where consistency and operational cost enter.
next: Take a 100 GB table and sketch four hash partitions, then trace a lookup by user ID.
Compare a localized query with a cross-partition aggregation and note what each must read.
Add replication to the sketch and mark which node serves reads after one partition owner fails.

leaderless-replication.problem: Leader-centric replication stops accepting writes when the master fails, so a system that cannot tolerate that outage needs a way to accept writes on any node without losing consistency.

terms.definition: The minimum number of nodes that must agree for a read or write to count.
terms.why: It replaces the leader's guarantee, letting the cluster decide success from a majority instead of one node.

terms.definition: The condition that the number of nodes acknowledging a write plus the number queried by a read exceeds the total replica count.
terms.why: It is the arithmetic that guarantees the read set and the latest write set share at least one node.

terms.definition: A per-record counter that increases with each successful write and identifies the newest value.
terms.why: Without a leader to order writes, it is what lets a reader pick the most recent response.

terms.definition: Nodes periodically exchanging what they hold with peers so a lagging node can discover and pull missed updates.
terms.why: It is how a node that was down during a write catches up without a special repair path.

arc: One leader makes write ordering simple and failure fatal
Fan out writes and wait for a majority
Read a majority and keep the highest version
Tune w and r, or delegate to a coordinator
leaderless-replication.primer: Three numbers and one rule carry the design: how many nodes acknowledge a write, how many answer a read, and how many replicas exist. Once those are clear, the rest of the cards follow from whether the read and write sets must overlap.
leaderless-replication.outro: Majority overlap gives strong consistency and removes the single point of failure, at the cost of contacting several nodes on every operation and carrying a version with each record. It does not make conflicts disappear; it makes the latest acknowledged value discoverable, while concurrent writes still need a resolution rule. The next questions are how to repair a lagging replica and when a coordinator should absorb the fan-out so clients stay simple.
next: Choose w, r and n for a five-node cluster and check whether w + r > n holds.
Simulate a write that reaches four nodes, then bring the fifth back and trace how gossip repairs it.
Compare client-driven fan-out with a coordinator for one read path and list what each client must know.

conflict-resolution.problem: Two masters can accept different updates to the same record, and something has to decide which version survives.

terms.definition: A rule that keeps the write with the latest stamp and discards the others.
terms.why: A single master gets this ordering for free, and every technique here is an attempt to rebuild it across nodes.

terms.definition: An identifier given to every write that no other write shares and that is always larger than any ID issued before it.
terms.why: Stamping writes with one makes last-write-wins deterministic without sending every write through a single node.

terms.definition: A ranking of masters in which the version from the highest-ranked node wins a conflict.
terms.why: It avoids running an ID generator at scale, but it orders nodes rather than writes.

terms.definition: Routing every write for a given record to the same master so updates to that record stay sequential.
terms.why: It is the cheapest option on the table because the conflict never happens.

arc: Parallel writes arrive with no shared order
Assign order with a global ID, a node rank, or a kept conflict
Cheap precedence can overwrite the true last write
Choose where to resolve, or route each record to one master
conflict-resolution.primer: Resolution is really a vocabulary for precedence: who or what gets to decide which of two versions is newer. That choice decides whether a conflict costs latency, throughput, or a user's data.
conflict-resolution.outro: Once writes carry an order, the cluster can converge without a single writer, and the policy moves into application code where the business meaning of a field is known. It does not recover intent that was never recorded: a rule that picks a winner still discards the loser. The next step is deciding, field by field, which merges can be automatic and which need a job or a person to look at both versions.
next: Write down, for each field your service writes, whether two versions merge as a union, a max, or need review.
Prototype a conflict table that keeps both versions and measure how long the reconciliation job takes to drain it.
Pick a routing key for record stickiness and check how evenly writes land across masters.

conflict-detection.problem: Two masters can each accept a write to the same record, and neither learns about the other until after both clients were told yes.

terms.definition: Two updates to the same record that no deterministic rule can reduce to a single value.
terms.why: Conflicts are structural in a multi-master cluster, so the question is which ones can be merged and which cannot.

terms.definition: Masters apply a write locally and send it to their peers later, after the client has already been acknowledged.
terms.why: That gap is what hides each write from the other master until sync time.

terms.definition: A merge that keeps every element present in either version, so nothing added on either side is lost.
terms.why: It is the correct answer for the shopping cart, where overwriting one version deletes a book the user added.

terms.definition: A setup where a master forwards each write to the other masters and waits for them before answering the client.
terms.why: It turns a silent conflict into one the cluster can see while the client is still waiting.

arc: Two masters accept the same record in parallel
Replication reveals the clash only after both writes succeeded
Additive data merges; a double booking cannot be undone
Sync propagation buys detection by giving up parallel writes
conflict-detection.primer: The shopping cart and the cinema seat are the same mechanism with different repair costs, which is why the vocabulary separates the clash itself from the merge rule and from when the cluster finds out.
conflict-detection.outro: Detection only helps where the invariant can be named: a set union is safe for a cart, while a seat sold twice has already broken a promise that no merge can restore. That pushes the hard cases earlier, into admission rules at write time, and leaves the mergeable ones to converge quietly. The next design question is which resources in a system are exclusive and therefore cannot be fixed after the fact.
next: Sort your schema's fields into additive (tags, cart items, follows) and exclusive (seat, username, inventory unit).
Reproduce the two-master cart example in a test and confirm the merge is a union rather than an overwrite.
For each exclusive resource, add a write-time guard before letting more than one node accept writes for it.

multi-master-replication.problem: A single master caps write throughput and forces distant clients to send every write to one region.

terms.definition: A setup in which several nodes accept client writes and forward them to each other, so no single node owns the write path.
terms.why: It is the alternative to funneling every write through one master, and it introduces the rest of this vocabulary.

terms.definition: A promise that copies will converge to the same value once replication finishes, with no promise about when.
terms.why: Asynchronous forwarding means a read can land on a master that has not seen the latest write yet.

terms.definition: Four guarantees a traditional database makes for a group of changes: all happen or none do, data stays valid, concurrent groups do not interfere, and finished changes survive a crash.
terms.why: Running a relational database this way gives those guarantees up.

terms.definition: A state where two parts of a cluster each act as the authority and accept writes independently.
terms.why: Normally a fault, it is the intended behaviour for shared documents and offline-first apps.

arc: One writer limits throughput and adds distance
Several masters take writes and replicate to each other
More capacity and locality, less ACID, more conflicts and traffic
Use it for throughput, failover, latency, or migration
multi-master-replication.primer: The vocabulary here is mostly about the bill: what a second writer buys, and which guarantees and resources it spends to do so.
multi-master-replication.outro: The pattern spreads as clients go offline, teams edit shared documents, and upgrades run two versions side by side. It does not produce a single truth: conflicts become a policy the application owns, and every write now travels to every peer. The next problem is the policy itself, which is why conflict detection and resolution follow directly from this design.
next: Measure peak writes per second against a single node's ceiling to see whether the write path is actually the bottleneck.
Draw a two-region topology and estimate replication traffic per write as master count grows.
For an upgrade, pair the old and new versions in a multi-master setup and shift a small share of production writes to the new one.

monotonic-reads.problem: Consecutive reads from one user can land on replicas at different points in the log, so the value appears to move backwards.

terms.definition: The delay between a write landing on the master and a replica applying it.
terms.why: Different replicas lag by different amounts, which is what makes two reads disagree.

terms.definition: A guarantee that one reader never sees a value older than one already observed, though it may still see a stale one.
terms.why: It is the weakest fix that stops the time-travel effect without making every read fresh.

terms.definition: Sending all of a given user's reads to the same replica.
terms.why: Each replica applies writes in order, so affinity converts that order into a per-user order.

arc: Replicas trail the master by different amounts
Random routing moves a reader between two points in the log
The displayed value oscillates while replicas catch up
Hash the user ID so each reader keeps one replica
monotonic-reads.primer: The mechanism is small once two ideas are separated: lag explains why copies differ, and affinity explains how to stop a single reader from sampling more than one copy.
monotonic-reads.outro: Affinity buys forward motion without coordination, because ordering is already guaranteed inside each replica. It does not buy freshness: a pinned reader can stay behind for as long as that replica lags. It also raises the next questions, which are what happens when the chosen replica dies and whether a user on a new device should keep the same affinity.
next: Log which replica served each read for a sample of users and count how often one user hits more than one.
Switch replica selection from random to a hash of user ID and compare the stale-read rate.
Kill the replica a test user is pinned to and decide whether reads should move or wait.

read-your-write-consistency.problem: A client writes a record and its next read is served by a replica that has not caught up, so the write looks lost.

terms.definition: A guarantee that after one client updates a record, that same client's later reads return the new value.
terms.why: It is a promise to the writer only, which is why it can be cheaper than global consistency.

terms.definition: The delay between a write landing on the master and a replica applying it.
terms.why: It is the whole cause: every fix works by sending the writer's read somewhere with no lag.

terms.definition: Routing a user's reads and writes to the master for a window after that user writes.
terms.why: It fixes the one user who notices without making every read pay for the master.

terms.definition: Pinning only the read paths that can expose a recent write, while other reads keep using replicas.
terms.why: It keeps the guarantee where users would notice while sparing the master in write-heavy systems.

arc: The write lands on the master, the read lands on a lagging replica
The user sees the old value and concludes the write failed
Synchronous replication closes the window and taxes every write
Pin the writer briefly, or only the reads that expose the write
read-your-write-consistency.primer: The options differ in how much traffic they send back to the master, so the useful distinction is between pinning a person, pinning a read path, and retrying on a miss.
read-your-write-consistency.outro: A per-client promise is much cheaper than making the whole cluster consistent, and it covers the failure users actually report. It does not help a second user, a second device, or a shared link, where the reader has no write of their own to anchor on. The next step is usually to measure lag and pinning cost against real traffic, then narrow the window and the read paths until the master load is acceptable.
next: List the reads a user hits within seconds of writing: profile, cart, order status, the item just edited.
Set the pin window from p99 replication lag and test it with lag injected deliberately.
Compare master load under full pinning and fragmented pinning on a write-heavy trace.

handling-outages-master-replica.problem: Replicas and masters crash routinely, and the recovery path decides whether an outage costs seconds or costs acknowledged writes.

terms.definition: A counter a replica stores on disk for the last operation it applied, so it knows where to resume.
terms.why: It turns recovery into a replay of the backlog instead of a fresh copy of the dataset.

terms.definition: A periodic signal that shows a node is alive, missed for longer than a set threshold to imply a crash.
terms.why: It is how the cluster notices a master is gone before it can start a promotion.

terms.definition: Replacing a failed master: noticing it is gone, choosing a replacement, and pointing clients at it.
terms.why: All three steps have to happen, or writes keep failing even with a healthy replacement available.

terms.definition: A second master that receives every write synchronously but serves no client traffic, kept ready to be promoted.
terms.why: It is the promotion target that cannot lose writes the old master had acknowledged.

arc: Assume a node dies after every operation
Replicas replay from a stored sequence number; masters are detected, replaced, announced
Promoting a lagging replica silently drops acknowledged writes
Keep a synchronous standby as the node you promote
handling-outages-master-replica.primer: The replica path and the master path use different vocabulary because they fail differently: one resumes a stream, the other changes who owns the write.
handling-outages-master-replica.outro: Failover restores the ability to accept writes, but only a synchronous copy guarantees the last writes survived. That extra idle machine is the price of a promotion that cannot lose data, which is why managed services carry it. The open questions move to the edges: how fast clients learn the new address, and how to stop an old master that comes back from accepting writes again.
next: Run a manual failover in staging and time each of the three steps separately.
Crash a replica and confirm it resumes from its stored sequence number instead of resyncing the dataset.
Add a synchronous passive standby to one cluster and measure the change in write latency.

replication-formats.problem: A replica has to reproduce a write exactly, and the log format decides whether that is compact or safe.

terms.definition: An ordered record of writes on the master that replicas pull and apply, also called a commit log or binlog.
terms.why: The format of its entries is the entire design choice.

terms.definition: The master logs the query it ran, and each replica executes the same query on its own copy.
terms.why: One entry can cover thousands of rows, which keeps the log small and auditable.

terms.definition: The master logs the rows that changed and their new values, and replicas apply those values directly.
terms.why: It replays safely even when the original query was not deterministic.

terms.definition: A function whose result can differ between runs or machines, such as UUID(), RAND() or NOW().
terms.why: Re-executing one on a replica produces a different value, and the copies diverge.

arc: The log must carry enough to reproduce the write
Record the statement, or record the rows it changed
Statements stay small but break on non-deterministic functions; rows replay safely but fan out
Choose the format that matches how deterministic your writes are
replication-formats.primer: The trade is between what the log stores and what the replica must be trusted to compute, so the two formats fail in opposite directions.
replication-formats.outro: Format choice settles replay safety but not timing: replicas still trail the master, and a row log grows with the number of changed rows rather than the number of statements. It also shifts cost between storage, log-lock time, and the risk of silent divergence. The practical next step is to find out how much of a real workload depends on functions that compute a fresh value each time.
next: Search a week of production statements for NOW(), RAND() and UUID() and count how many writes depend on them.
Measure log growth per thousand writes under both formats on a copy of the data.
Take one bulk update and compare a single statement entry with the row count it expands to.

replication-strategies.problem: A write can be acknowledged before or after its copies exist, and that single choice sets durability and throughput.

terms.definition: The master waits for every replica to confirm the write before answering the client.
terms.why: It makes lag zero at the cost of every write waiting for the slowest replica.

terms.definition: The master answers the client immediately and sends the change to replicas in the background.
terms.why: It maximizes throughput and leaves a window where acknowledged data exists on one machine only.

terms.definition: The master waits for confirmation from a subset of replicas, often one, and lets the rest catch up later.
terms.why: It buys durability with a marginal latency cost, which is why it sits between the other two.

terms.definition: The promise that a write the client was told succeeded survives a crash of the machine that took it.
terms.why: It is exactly what asynchronous replication risks and what the synchronous copy protects.

arc: Replication serves availability, recovery, read scale and locality
The strategy decides how long a write waits for its copies
Waiting for all risks a full stall; waiting for none risks lost writes
Wait for one replica and let the rest lag
replication-strategies.primer: All three start the same way, with the master updating its own copy, so the vocabulary is entirely about what happens between that moment and the client's acknowledgement.
replication-strategies.outro: The setting is usually configurable per store, so the decision can follow the criticality of the data rather than a global default. It does not remove the underlying lag: it only chooses who pays for it, the writer in latency or the system in possible loss. Replica placement then becomes part of the latency budget, because the wait is set by the slowest node in the confirmed set.
next: Split your writes into those that must survive a master crash and those that can be recomputed.
Measure p99 write latency under all three strategies on the same hardware.
Configure one synchronous replica, kill the master, and check that no acknowledged write is missing.

master-replica-replication.problem: Reads outgrow a single machine while writes still need one order.

terms.definition: A setup where every node holds a full copy of the data but only one node, the master, accepts writes.
terms.why: It is the baseline pattern that the other replication designs react to.

terms.definition: An ordered record of changes on the master that replicas pull and apply, such as a binlog or commit log.
terms.why: It is how a write reaches the nodes that did not accept it.

terms.definition: The time between the master committing a write and a replica applying it.
terms.why: It bounds how stale a read can be and is the metric operators watch continuously.

terms.definition: The process by which healthy replicas agree on which one becomes the new master.
terms.why: It is how the cluster recovers the write path after the master dies, without restoring from backup.

arc: Every node holds a full copy, but only one takes writes
Reads fan out across replicas; writes queue behind the master
Read capacity grows with nodes; write capacity and failure tolerance do not
Add replicas for reads and rehearse promoting one
master-replica-replication.primer: The pattern is simple enough that most of its behaviour follows from two numbers: how many replicas serve reads, and how far behind the master they are allowed to fall.
master-replica-replication.outro: This design makes read scaling almost linear while leaving the write path as the ceiling and the failure point. Lag and promotion are the two places where that shows up, which is why the follow-on problems are stale reads and failover rather than throughput. The next step is to know the read-to-write ratio and the worst-case lag before adding nodes or changing strategy.
next: Compute the read-to-write ratio and estimate how many replicas the read side needs.
Chart replication lag for a day and record its p99.
Run a leader election in a test cluster and time how long writes fail.

durability.problem: A database can acknowledge a committed transaction and still lose it if the change exists only in memory when the machine dies.

terms.definition: The guarantee that a transaction the database has acknowledged as committed survives a crash, restart, or power loss.
terms.why: Durability is the promise the other three ACID properties depend on, and the one that decides whether an acknowledged purchase still exists after an outage.

terms.definition: An append-only file where the database records a change before applying it to the main data, so the change can be replayed after a crash.
terms.why: The log is the mechanism that makes a disk write on every commit cheap enough to afford.

terms.definition: A commit protocol in which a coordinator first asks every participating database whether it can commit, and only tells them to commit after all have said yes.
terms.why: Two-phase commit is how the same promise is extended across databases that must commit together, and why a distributed commit is only as strong as its weakest participant.

arc: Commit succeeds, then the machine dies
Log intent before touching the data
Recovery replays the log to the last consistent state
A distributed commit inherits the weakest participant
durability.primer: The promise sounds simple until you ask where the bytes are at the instant of commit. These terms separate the guarantee, the log that makes it affordable, and the coordination that carries it across machines.
durability.outro: Local durability moves the hard part to distribution, because a coordinator can only promise what every participant has already made safe. Replication, disk failure, and the gap between a write reaching the operating system's buffer and reaching durable storage decide whether the promise holds under a real outage. Once the log exists, it also becomes a source for recovery, replication, and change streams, so the structure that survives a crash earns a second job.
next: Trace one commit through the database log and confirm the caller is acknowledged only after the log record is on durable storage.
Kill the process mid-transaction in a staging copy and verify recovery keeps committed rows and discards uncommitted ones.
Read the two-phase commit failure cases, especially a coordinator crash after the participants have prepared.

isolation.problem: Two concurrent transactions can read and overwrite each other's unfinished work, so the result depends on timing rather than on the rules.

terms.definition: The guarantee that concurrent transactions leave the same result as if they had run one at a time.
terms.why: Isolation is the property that keeps a flash sale from selling the same unit twice.

terms.definition: A group of reads and writes that the database treats as one unit, ending in either a commit or a rollback.
terms.why: The transaction is the unit whose intermediate states must stay invisible to everyone else.

terms.definition: A marker a transaction places on a row so other transactions must wait; shared locks let other readers in, exclusive locks do not.
terms.why: Locks are how the engine turns concurrent writers into an order, at the cost of waiting.

terms.definition: A setting that decides how strictly transactions are separated, from running one at a time to letting them see each other's uncommitted work.
terms.why: The isolation level is the dial that decides how much waiting the workload pays for.

arc: Two buyers check the last slot at once
Locks serialize the conflicting writers
Strictness buys correctness and costs concurrency
Pick the level the workload can afford
isolation.primer: Isolation is easier to reason about once the players have names: the unit of work, the object it holds, and the setting that decides how long it holds it. The arc follows one contended row from check to commit.
isolation.outro: The next question is which level a workload actually needs, because strict isolation can turn a busy system into a queue. Distributed transactions add a second layer, where locks or conflicts span machines and retries become part of normal operation. Deadlocks and contention are the price of blocking, which is why many systems shorten transactions and push coordination outward.
next: Open two database sessions and reproduce a lost update on the same row, first without a transaction and then inside one.
Set the isolation level to each of the four settings and record which anomalies disappear and what contention appears.
Shorten one long transaction and measure the change in lock wait time.

atomicity.problem: A multi-step transaction can stop halfway, leaving a debit without its credit and a balance that no one intended.

terms.definition: The rule that a transaction's statements either all take effect or none of them do, so no observer ever sees a partial result.
terms.why: Atomicity is what makes the debit-without-credit failure impossible to observe.

terms.definition: A group of database statements that the engine applies as one unit and can undo as one unit.
terms.why: The transaction is the scope inside which the all-or-nothing rule applies.

terms.definition: Undoing a transaction's partial changes so the database returns to the state it had before the transaction started.
terms.why: Rollback is the path that removes a half-applied transaction after a failure.

terms.definition: A hardware operation that either completes entirely or has no effect, such as compare-and-swap, which changes a value only if it still equals an expected value.
terms.why: Atomic instructions are the smallest all-or-nothing steps from which every larger guarantee is assembled.

arc: A transfer has a dangerous middle
Log the start and the end
Recovery finishes committed work and erases unfinished work
Build bigger guarantees from smaller atomic steps
atomicity.primer: All-or-nothing is a property, but it is implemented by smaller pieces that are themselves all-or-nothing. The terms move from the transaction down to the instruction that makes the guarantee possible.
atomicity.outro: The same pattern scales upward: a business process that spans two services needs its own record of intent, because no database lock covers the gap between them. That is where sagas, idempotent retries, and compensating actions enter, each trying to make a distributed middle unobservable. The smaller the atomic primitive, the more the larger guarantee costs to build.
next: Write a two-statement transfer and kill the process between the statements, then confirm the database has no half-applied state.
Find how the engine implements rollback, whether through an undo log or a saved copy, and read that code path.
Replace one read-modify-write in application code with a compare-and-swap or a conditional update.

consistency.problem: Rules that live only in application code can be bypassed by any other writer, so the data drifts away from the business's own invariants.

terms.definition: The guarantee that every committed transaction leaves the data satisfying the rules declared to the database.
terms.why: Consistency is the property that makes the database's rules hold after every commit, not just after a careful code path.

terms.definition: A rule that must hold in every valid state of the data, such as an account balance never being negative.
terms.why: An invariant is the thing the schema protects, regardless of which transaction ran last.

terms.definition: A rule declared in the database schema, such as requiring a referenced row to exist or a number to stay positive, that the engine checks on every write.
terms.why: Constraints are how an invariant stops depending on which service wrote the row.

terms.definition: An automatic follow-up change, such as deleting a parent's children, that the database performs as part of the same transaction.
terms.why: Cascades are how a change to one row carries its required follow-up changes into the same commit.

arc: Rules live in one service, other writers bypass them
Declare the invariant in the schema
Cascades extend the commit and its cost
Choose synchronous correctness or leaner transactions
consistency.primer: Correctness only means something once the rules are written down where the database can see them. The vocabulary here is about declaring those rules and paying for their enforcement.
consistency.outro: Declared invariants are only as strong as the writers that go through the database, because a service that writes around the schema reintroduces the problem. In a distributed system the same word also describes replica agreement, which is a different guarantee and a frequent source of confusion. The practical path is to enumerate the rules, push the checkable ones into the schema, and reserve application logic for the rules the database cannot express.
next: List three rules the business relies on and mark which ones can be expressed as constraints or cascades.
Add a check constraint or foreign key to a staging table and try to write a violating row.
Time a transaction with a synchronous cascade and decide whether the correctness is worth the extra commit latency.

architectures-in-distributed-systems.problem: Teams choose a topology by counting tiers instead of deciding where business logic lives and who owns state, then find the choice expensive to reverse.

terms.definition: A two-part arrangement where a client asks a server that holds the data, and the client is smart enough to shape and present the answer.
terms.why: Client-server is the baseline arrangement the other three are measured against.

terms.definition: An arrangement with a stateless client, a middle layer that holds the business logic, and a server that holds the data.
terms.why: Three-tier is the move that makes the client replaceable by putting logic in the middle.

terms.definition: An extension of three-tier where the middle layer calls other services, each with its own logic and often its own data.
terms.why: N-tier is what three-tier becomes when the middle layer is itself a network of services.

terms.definition: A decentralized arrangement where every machine can act as both client and server, with no special node holding all the responsibility.
terms.why: Peer-to-peer is the alternative that removes the special node entirely, which is why it is hard to adopt later.

arc: Ask where logic lives and who owns state
Move rules out of the client into a middle layer
Let the middle layer become a network of services
Decentralize at inception or not at all
architectures-in-distributed-systems.primer: The useful question is not how many boxes a diagram has, but which box is allowed to be smart and which one owns the data. The four topologies are stages along that single decision.
architectures-in-distributed-systems.outro: Each step toward distribution buys independence and pays in coordination, because the middle layer becomes a network and a network becomes a system with partial failure. Microservices make ownership explicit but turn every cross-service read into a latency and consistency decision. Peer-to-peer removes the special node, which is why it works best when the protocol, not an operator, can define correctness.
next: Draw one request path and mark every place business logic runs and every place state is stored.
Move one rule from a client into the middle layer and note what no longer has to be shipped.
For an existing service, write down which data it owns and which reads it makes into another service's data.

mistaken-beliefs-of-distributed-systems.problem: A design built on the assumption that the network is reliable, fast, secure, and uniform fails at the first real network.

terms.definition: The time a message spends travelling from one machine to another, which distance and the speed of light set a floor under.
terms.why: Latency is the limit that no amount of code removes, only hides.

terms.definition: The amount of data a link can carry in a given time; it is finite on the machine, on the wire, and at the receiver.
terms.why: Bandwidth is the resource that becomes both a bottleneck and a bill.

terms.definition: The actual set of links and devices a packet crosses, which changes when hardware or software fails.
terms.why: Topology is why a sudden change in timing is evidence, not noise.

terms.definition: A named set of false assumptions, such as the network being reliable, fast, and secure, that designers new to distributed systems tend to make.
terms.why: The fallacies are the checklist that turns each assumption into an explicit countermeasure.

arc: LAN assumptions become quiet defaults
Each fallacy needs an explicit countermeasure
Geography, bandwidth, and cost set hard limits
Monitor the path, not just the endpoints
mistaken-beliefs-of-distributed-systems.primer: Most distributed-system failures start as assumptions that were never written down, so they were never tested. The terms name the physical limits and the false defaults that a design has to disprove.
mistaken-beliefs-of-distributed-systems.outro: The physical limits do not go away with better tooling; they move into the bill and the tail latency. That makes observability part of the design rather than an afterthought, because bytes, path, and timing have to be measured where the traffic actually goes. Once those measurements exist, capacity planning, encryption, and failure testing become concrete rather than aspirational.
next: Compute the round-trip latency floor for the two farthest regions you serve from the distance between them.
Instrument one service for bytes in, bytes out, and cost per request, then compare that with its latency graph.
Take each fallacy in turn and write the countermeasure the system currently relies on, or note that none exists.

fork-bomb.problem: Any system that runs untrusted code can be taken down by a few lines that create processes until the machine can create no more.

terms.definition: The operating-system call that creates a new process by copying the calling process.
terms.why: Fork is the call that turns one process into two, which is all the attack needs.

terms.definition: A running program with its own memory and its own place in the scheduler's queue.
terms.why: A process is the resource the machine runs out of first.

terms.definition: An attack that makes a system unusable for legitimate users by consuming a resource it needs, such as CPU, memory, or process slots.
terms.why: Denial of service is the outcome: the machine is alive but cannot do useful work.

terms.definition: An operating-system limit on how many processes one user may have running at once, set with `ulimit -u`.
terms.why: The process cap is the single limit that converts exponential growth into a failed call.

arc: Fork until the machine refuses
Each child copies itself and forks again
The system loses the ability to start processes
Cap processes per user
fork-bomb.primer: A fork bomb is short enough to type in one line, which is why the vocabulary matters more than the code. The terms describe the resource being exhausted and the single limit that stops it.
fork-bomb.outro: The same failure appears wherever a shared machine runs code it did not write: build agents, evaluation sandboxes, and container hosts. A per-user cap protects the host but not a neighbor on the same kernel, so isolation has to match the trust boundary. The durable fix is to treat process creation, memory, and time as budgets that every untrusted job must fit inside.
next: Run the shell one-liner in a disposable virtual machine with a low `ulimit -u` and watch forks fail instead of the machine freezing.
Check the process limit for the user and for the container that runs untrusted code, and confirm they match the trust boundary.
Add a process cap and a wall-clock timeout to any code evaluator before running the next submission.

chained-operators-python.problem: The same expression `a < b < c` means conjunction in Python and a nested comparison in C, so identical-looking code returns different answers.

terms.definition: An expression such as `a < b < c` that Python treats as `(a < b) and (b < c)`, evaluating the shared middle value once.
terms.why: Chained comparison is the syntax whose meaning differs between Python and C.

terms.definition: Stopping an expression as soon as its result is settled, so the remaining parts never run.
terms.why: Short-circuiting is why the later operands may never execute, which matters when they have side effects.

terms.definition: The instruction sequence the Python compiler emits for the interpreter to execute, one operation at a time.
terms.why: Bytecode is where the shared middle operand and the early exit become visible.

terms.definition: The interpreter's working area, where instructions push values and pop them back off.
terms.why: The operand stack is the workspace where the duplicate is parked for the next comparison.

arc: Same symbols, different languages, different answers
Compile a chain around one shared middle value
Jump out at the first false link
Disassemble before trusting intuition about cost
chained-operators-python.primer: The syntax is familiar, but the meaning is decided by the compiler and the stack, not by the symbols. The terms connect the written expression to the instructions that actually run.
chained-operators-python.outro: Language semantics turn out to be a small number of code-generation choices, which means they can be read, changed, and broken like any other code. That is useful for understanding a version's behavior and dangerous for assuming it will never change. The same habit, reading bytecode before reasoning about cost, applies to comprehensions, generators, and other constructs where the syntax hides a loop.
next: Disassemble `a < b < c` and `6 > 7 > 8` with `dis`, then walk the stack by hand until the jump makes sense.
Rewrite one repeated comparison into a chain and confirm the middle expression is evaluated only once when it has a side effect.
Remove the `DUP_TOP` and `ROT_THREE` lines from `compiler_compare` in a scratch CPython build and compare `-3 < -2 < -1`.

taxonomy-on-sql.problem: Storing one table per hierarchy level turns every new depth into a schema migration and every breadcrumb into a query per level.

terms.definition: A tree stored as rows that each point to their parent, so the depth of the tree is data rather than a fixed set of tables.
terms.why: The adjacency list is the design that keeps depth in a column instead of in the table count.

terms.definition: A query that uses the same table more than once under different names, so one row can be compared with another row in that table.
terms.why: The self-join is how a fixed maximum depth becomes one query rather than a loop in application code.

terms.definition: A SQL calculation that looks at a group of related rows and returns a value for each row, such as numbering children within each parent.
terms.why: The window function is how top-k per category becomes one query rather than one query per category.

terms.definition: An index built on two or more columns in a fixed order, which lets a query filter on the first column and sort by the second without a separate sort.
terms.why: The composite index is how the children query avoids sorting the whole table on every render.

arc: One table per level hardens today's depth
Collapse the tree into parent_id and type
A fixed-depth self-join beats one query per level
Rank children per parent and index for the query
taxonomy-on-sql.primer: A hierarchy looks like a schema problem until the product adds a level and the queries multiply. The vocabulary here is about storing depth as data and making each page cost one query instead of one per level.
